title: PART I

nodes.title: Boeing Business and Major Segments
nodes.summary: Boeing is a major aerospace company organized into four reportable segments: Commercial Airplanes, Defense, Space & Security, Global Services, and Boeing Capital. Commercial Airplanes develops, produces, markets, and supports aircraft, including 737, 747, 767, 777, and 787 models, with 777X and 737 MAX derivatives in development. Defense, Space & Security develops military aircraft, weapons, defense and intelligence systems, satellites, and space services. Its principal customer is the U.S. Department of Defense, which generated about 84% of 2021 segment revenue; other customers include NASA and international defense and satellite markets. Products span fixed-wing and rotary-wing aircraft, unmanned vehicles, space and missile systems, and related programs and joint ventures.

nodes.title: Services, Financing, and Intellectual Property
nodes.summary: Global Services provides commercial and defense customers worldwide with aerospace support, including logistics, engineering, maintenance, upgrades, parts, training, documentation, and digital services. Boeing Capital finances customer purchases and manages exposure through leases, receivables, sale or re-lease assets, and investments. Boeing owns and licenses patents and other intellectual property; government contracts may grant the U.S. government rights to use inventions. Research and engineering expertise, trademarks, and trade secrets also support its businesses, though no single IP right or license is considered materially critical.

nodes.title: Human Capital
nodes.summary: Boeing describes its COVID-19 response, including vaccination support, virtual care and work, site safety, health reporting and contact tracing overseen by a crisis group. At year-end 2021, it had about 142,000 employees, including 47,000 union members, with major union representation and agreement timelines noted. It outlines diversity, equity and inclusion efforts and workforce demographics; competitive benefits, hiring and retention; employee feedback and recognition; professional development and education; and commitments to safety, ethics, accountability and addressing concerns.

nodes.title: Competition
nodes.summary: The commercial aircraft market faces intense global competition, including Airbus and entrants from Russia, China, and Japan; the company emphasizes process improvements, cost reduction, and product quality. Boeing Defense, Space & Security competes across segments with major U.S. and international firms, including rivals that sometimes team up, and expects strong competition through 2022. Boeing Global Services faces similarly tough commercial and defense services markets, offers lifecycle services from training and logistics to maintenance, upgrades, and daily operations, and aims to grow 2022 market share through customer satisfaction and productivity.

nodes.title: Regulatory Matters
nodes.summary: The text describes extensive U.S. and international regulation, including government contract termination rights and resulting payment or liability, FAA and foreign aviation certification and safety requirements, and environmental compliance and remediation risks, including potentially responsible party liability and possible material financial effects. Non-U.S. sales face trade, investment, currency, political, economic, and anti-corruption rules and risks. The business also relies on qualified sources of key aerospace materials, often sole-source parts, and many suppliers and affordable energy; disruptions or failures could harm production, profitability, and customer commitments.

nodes.title: Environmental, International Sales, and Supply Risks
nodes.summary: The page discusses environmental regulations, compliance and remediation costs, potential climate-related requirements, and joint and several liability for contaminated sites, including possible contribution from other responsible parties. It notes that non-U.S. sales face regulatory, procurement, currency, political and economic risks. Aerospace production depends on key materials, parts and subcontractors, some sole-source, whose qualification or failure may affect schedules and profitability; affordable energy is also essential.

Item 1A. Risk Factors
An investment in our common stock or debt securities involves risks and uncertainties and our actual results and future trends may differ materially from our past or projected future performance. We urge investors to consider carefully the risk factors described below in evaluating the information contained in this report.

nodes.title: Risks Related to COVID-19
nodes.summary: COVID-19 and future public-health crises pose risks to the company’s business, finances, operations and cash flow through reduced demand and air traffic, supply-chain instability, customer distress and possible government mandates. Operational risks include shutdowns, absenteeism, restrictions, shortages, delays and higher costs; prior site closures and supplier shortages could recur. Liquidity risks include substantial cash use and debt, expected negative operating cash flow, potential financing difficulties, late customer payments and credit-rating impacts. Airline capacity cuts threaten customer viability, aircraft orders, deliveries, remarketing and program earnings, while uncertain recovery and lasting industry changes may weaken demand and pressure suppliers. The pandemic also increased tax valuation allowances and may intensify labor and other risks.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Our Business and Operations
Risks Related to Our Business and Operations (intro)
nodes.summary: The text outlines ongoing 737 MAX risks: remaining global certification and return-to-service steps, production and delivery delays, supplier and supply-chain problems, customer concessions, and uncertainty in financial estimates. The 2019 grounding and production suspension reduced revenue, margins and cash flow and increased costs; further delays could disrupt production, require workforce or production-plan changes, and worsen results. Boeing faces accident-related lawsuits, government and SEC investigations, and a DOJ Deferred Prosecution Agreement, for which it expensed $744 million in Q4 2020. Customer concessions and related considerations totaled $2.9 billion at year-end 2021, including $0.7 billion under negotiation. Changes in production, pricing, costs, warranties, investigations, delivery timing, supplier health or customer negotiations could materially affect financial results and cash flows.

nodes.title: In addition to the impact of COVID-19 described above, our Commercial Airplanes and Global Services businesses depend heavily on commercial airlines, and are subject to unique risks.
key_items: Market conditions have a significant impact on demand for our commercial aircraft and related services

nodes.summary: Commercial Airplanes and Global Services face risks tied to airline-dependent demand and volatile market conditions. Long-term traffic growth depends on economic growth and political stability, while aircraft demand is affected by airline profitability, financing, trade and government relations, technology, competition, fuel costs, terrorism, epidemics and regulation. Industry downturns or customer distress can reduce, delay or cancel orders and payments, lowering revenue, profits, cash flow and backlog, with effects potentially extending across years of scheduled deliveries. Firm fixed-price contracts use indexed escalation clauses; unpredictable index changes and cost overruns exceeding escalation can hurt revenue and margins. Revenue is concentrated among a limited number of airlines, and customers may not exercise options or meet commitments; fleet changes, consolidation or financial difficulties can further reduce sales and profit opportunities.

nodes.title: Our Commercial Airplanes business depends on our ability to maintain a healthy production system, ensure every airplane in our production system conforms to our exacting specification, achieve planned production rate targets, successfully develop new aircraft or new derivative aircraft, and meet or exceed stringent performance and reliability standards.
key_items: We must minimize disruption caused by production changes, achieve operational stability and implement productivity improvements in order to meet customer demand and maintain our profitability

Operational challenges impacting the production system for one or more of our commercial aircraft programs could result in production delays and/or failure to meet customer demand for new aircraft, either of which would negatively impact our revenues and operating margins

nodes.summary: Boeing’s commercial-aircraft business relies on stable production, quality, on-time rates, successful aircraft development, and meeting performance and reliability standards amid complex supplier, workforce, and regulatory demands. Tighter certification rules may raise costs; new programs face schedule risks. The 737 MAX grounding disrupted operations, while 787 quality issues caused delivery pauses, inspections, rework, and FAA discussions; 777X, 737 MAX, and 787 delays may trigger customer compensation, order changes, or cancellations. Production adjustments, low 787 rates, supplier constraints, and process changes threaten delivery schedules and program results. Operational defects or approval delays can increase costs, disrupt production, impair aircraft performance, and raise warranty or support expenses; failure to meet reliability requirements could reduce revenue and profitability.

nodes.title: Changes in levels of U.S. government defense spending or overall acquisition priorities could negatively impact our financial position and results of operations.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks to financial results from unpredictable U.S. defense spending, delayed or temporary appropriations, shifting acquisition priorities, budget cuts, and changing DoD procurement demands, including COVID-19 compliance costs. It describes dependence on subcontractors, suppliers, and raw materials, whose disruption, financial problems, or price increases could delay delivery or raise costs. Intense domestic and international competition may reduce contracts, revenue, and market share. Significant non-U.S. sales expose the company to international risks, including regulatory changes, executive actions, trade disputes, and tariffs or penalties.

nodes.title: Procurement, Supplier, and Competitive Risks
key_items: Our ability to deliver products and services that satisfy customer requirements is heavily dependent on the performance and financial stability of our subcontractors and suppliers, as well as on the availability of raw materials and other components.
Competition within our markets and with respect to the products we sell may reduce our future contracts and sales.
nodes.summary: Changing government acquisition policies and insufficient federal funding for COVID-19 compliance costs may reduce revenue, market share, and government purchasing power. Delivery depends on suppliers and subcontractors, whose financial or performance problems, disruptions, single-source dependencies, or shortages and high prices for materials could cause delays, missed commitments, or higher costs. Intense competition—including from international aircraft manufacturers and amid defense consolidation, shifting budgets, and cost pressures—could reduce contracts, sales, revenue, and market share.

nodes.title: We derive a significant portion of our revenues from non-U.S. sales and are subject to the risks of doing business in other countries.
nodes.summary: Non-U.S. customers, including foreign military sales, generated about 37% of revenue in 2021 and are expected to remain significant. International business risks include regulatory and executive changes; trade disputes, tariffs and penalties; government policies, local-spending and industrial participation requirements; currency and political or economic volatility affecting orders; reliance on foreign representatives; customer financing and credit uncertainty; taxes, export controls, embargoes, sanctions and other restrictions; managing operations across countries; and compliance with U.S. and foreign laws. Terrorism, war, epidemics and international tensions may also disrupt business. These factors are unpredictable and could harm operations, financial position, results or cash flows; U.S.-China tariffs and deteriorating trade relations pose particular risks given China’s importance to airplane sales and backlog.

nodes.title: We use estimates in accounting for many contracts and programs. Changes in our estimates could adversely affect our future financial results.
nodes.summary: The text explains that contract and program accounting relies on estimates of risks, revenues, costs, schedules, technical issues, labor and material inflation, performance incentives or penalties, supplier claims, and award fees; changes can harm future results. For commercial aircraft, costs are accumulated by program and recognized as units are delivered, requiring estimates of program quantity, duration, prices, production and tooling costs, and warranty costs. Orders, market studies, customer and model mix, production rates and learning curves, escalation, derivatives, supplier performance and negotiations, claims, and certification issues can change these estimates. Development programs such as the 777X also face certification-timing risks across jurisdictions. Different assumptions or changed circumstances may materially alter reported sales and profits; the text refers readers to further accounting-policy disclosures.

nodes.title: We may not realize the anticipated benefits of mergers, acquisitions, joint ventures/strategic alliances or divestitures.
nodes.summary: Mergers, acquisitions, joint ventures, alliances, and divestitures may fail to deliver expected benefits. Outcomes depend on integration, portfolio and personnel performance, and partner performance; adverse effects may include legacy liabilities, transaction and intangible amortization costs, asset impairments, guarantees, indemnifications, or changes from joint venture consolidation. Despite risk-mitigation processes, success is not assured. Divestitures may leave ongoing financial obligations, with nonperformance potentially causing payments, higher costs, or write-downs.

The section covers risks from the 737 MAX’s certification, production and delivery delays, supplier problems, customer concessions, litigation and investigations, and uncertain financial estimates. It describes airline-demand volatility, customer concentration, fixed-price contract exposure, production quality and reliability challenges, new-aircraft development and certification risks, and possible effects on orders, costs, revenue and cash flow. It also addresses changing U.S. defense budgets and priorities, supplier and competitive pressures, international sales and geopolitical, regulatory, trade, financing and compliance risks, reliance on estimates in contract and program accounting, and uncertainty that mergers, acquisitions, joint ventures, alliances or divestitures will deliver expected benefits.

Climate change, ESG expectations, physical impacts, supply-chain disruptions, emissions and other environmental requirements may increase costs, restrict products or operations, affect competitiveness and reputation, and impede long-term goals. nodes.title: Overview
nodes.summary: Boeing is a global aerospace and defense leader, operating mainly in the U.S. while expanding internationally through partners and suppliers. Its businesses span commercial aircraft, defense, space, services, and customer financing. Its strategy emphasizes strong core operations, market-responsive products, efficiency, quality, growth, and shareholder returns. Commercial Airplanes targets leadership through safe, efficient, valuable aircraft and services; Defense, Space & Security delivers affordable solutions and pursues next-generation programs and growth in adjacent and international markets; Global Services supports commercial and defense customers; Boeing Capital arranges selective customer financing.

nodes.title: Business Environment and Trends
nodes.summary: In 2021, COVID-19, 787 production problems and rework, and lingering 737 MAX effects harmed Boeing’s business. Air travel recovered unevenly to about 40% of 2019 traffic; domestic and narrow-body demand should rebound faster than international and wide-body markets, while freighters benefit from strong cargo demand. Airline losses, liquidity preservation, delivery deferrals, reduced spending, and cancellations constrain near-term demand. Boeing expects travel to regain 2019 levels in 2023–24, has cut production rates, anticipates the first 777X delivery in late 2023, and faces risks from inventory deliveries and further rate cuts. The 737 MAX has returned to service in most countries, with China deliveries anticipated in 2022 pending approval; 787 deliveries remain paused during rework and FAA discussions. Long term, Boeing projects 4% annual traffic growth and demand for about 43,610 aircraft over 20 years, while noting industry risks. A federal funding deadline could disrupt operations. BGS commercial services remain weak, while government services demand is stable; BDS demand is healthy despite pandemic-related disruptions. Supplier shortages, liquidity pressures, and operational disruption hurt productivity and financial results. Boeing is improving processes to strengthen resilience, liquidity, and competitiveness.

nodes.title: Total Costs and Expenses (“Cost of Sales”)
nodes.summary: Cost of sales includes materials, labor, overhead, and subcontracting; BCA primarily uses program accounting for commercial airplanes, long-term contract costs are recognized as incurred, and commercial spare parts use average cost. Cost of sales was $59.269 billion (95.2% of revenue) in 2021, $63.843 billion (109.8%) in 2020, and $72.093 billion (94.2%) in 2019. The 2021 decline reflected higher 2020 segment charges, partly offset by increased revenue and the 787 reach-forward loss; the 2020 decline reflected lower revenue, partly offset by program, pandemic, production, and severance charges. The text also reports R&D by segment: $2.249 billion in 2021, $2.476 billion in 2020, and $3.219 billion in 2019. R&D fell mainly because of reduced product-development investment and 777X spending in 2021, and lower BCA and Boeing NeXt spending in 2020.

nodes.title: Backlog
nodes.summary: The table reports Boeing’s 2021 and 2020 backlog by business segment and distinguishes contractual from unobligated backlog. Contractual backlog excludes options, unsigned announced orders, terminable orders, and unfunded government contracts. Its 2021 increase reflected new orders, reclassifications, price escalation, and accounting-related adjustments, partly offset by deliveries and cancellations. Delivery delays and possible extended 737 MAX pauses, China restrictions, or delayed aircraft entry into service could reduce backlog or cause cancellations; COVID-19 may also weaken orders. Unobligated backlog declined mainly due to reclassifications, partly offset by contract awards.

nodes.title: Additional Considerations
nodes.summary: Boeing monitors global trade and geopolitical developments, including COVID-19’s adverse effects on the economy, aerospace demand and commercial-aircraft orders; U.S.-China tensions and tariffs; U.S. steel and aluminum tariffs and trade agreements with Mexico, Canada and the EU; potential U.S.-Russia sanctions and export restrictions; and U.S.-EU/U.K. aircraft-subsidy disputes, whose tariffs were suspended under cooperative frameworks. Commercial Airplanes faces a pandemic-disrupted, highly competitive market, with roughly 80% of backlog tied to non-U.S. airlines. The 737 MAX grounding weakened delivery share, while Airbus and other state-supported rivals expand and improve products, intensifying pricing pressure. Boeing aims to improve products and services, transform its business and counter unfair subsidies.

nodes.title: Revenues
nodes.summary: BCA revenue rose $3.331 billion in 2021 versus 2020, mainly from increased 737 MAX deliveries and no repeat of 2020 customer-consideration charges, partly offset by fewer 787 deliveries. Revenue fell $16.093 billion in 2020 versus 2019 amid pandemic impacts, 787 production issues and the MAX grounding, partly offset by lower MAX-related charges. MAX deliveries resumed in December 2020; most non-U.S. jurisdictions had approved its return by year-end 2021. 787 deliveries were paused from May 2021, and revenue depends on MAX ramp-up, 787 resumption and industry recovery. The text also tabulates annual and cumulative 2019–2021 deliveries for the 737, 747, 767, 777, 787 and total, with notes identifying intercompany deliveries and aircraft treated as operating leases in consolidation.

nodes.title: Loss From Operations
nodes.summary: BCA’s operating loss narrowed to $6.475 billion in 2021 from $13.847 billion in 2020, reflecting a $3.460 billion 787 reach-forward loss and abnormal 737 MAX and 787 production costs, partly offset by higher MAX deliveries. The 2020 loss, versus $6.657 billion in 2019, included a $6.493 billion 777X reach-forward loss, pandemic-related delivery and margin declines, MAX costs and customer considerations, severance, 737NG repairs, temporary shutdown costs, and lower 787 margins; reduced R&D spending partly offset these factors. The 2019 loss mainly reflected no MAX deliveries in three quarters and $8.259 billion in estimated customer considerations. Pandemic effects and low deliveries are expected to hurt future earnings and margins until deliveries recover.

nodes.title: Backlog
nodes.summary: Defines backlog as probable-to-collect transaction prices for unsatisfied obligations without outstanding customer-controlled contingencies, excluding options, BCC orders, and terminable orders; explains contractual relief, ASC 606 adjustments, and order changes. BCA backlog rose from $281.6 billion in 2020 to $296.9 billion in 2021 despite $27.5 billion in cancellations, with risks from delivery pauses, program delays, and COVID-19. Defines program accounting quantity, its role in estimating margins, and quarterly review, then provides 2019–2021 program quantities, undelivered firm orders, and cumulative firm orders, with notes on military derivatives, BCC aircraft, and 777X.

nodes.title: Program Highlights
nodes.summary: The text reviews commercial-aircraft program status and risks. The 737 and 767 accounting quantities grew in 2021; the 767 produces three aircraft monthly and has near break-even commercial margins. The 747 is produced at 0.5 monthly, with production expected to end in late 2022 without material financial impact. The 777 quantity increased; combined 777/777X production is expected to rise to three monthly in 2022. The 777X, including new variants and a freighter offering, targets first delivery in late 2023 after certification and design delays, a $6.5 billion reach-forward loss, and near break-even margins; further losses remain possible. The 787’s deliveries remain paused amid quality issues and rework; production is very low, with about $2 billion in cumulative abnormal costs expected and a $3.5 billion 2021 fourth-quarter loss. Delivery resumption, rates, and further losses depend on rework, FAA activity, customers, suppliers, and demand, especially in China. Fleet support services span aircraft operation and lifecycle support; costs are expensed and historically about 1% of consolidated product and service costs. Development timelines list the MAX 7 (2011–2022), MAX 10 (2017–2023), and 777X (2013–2023), subject to certification uncertainty.

nodes.title: Additional Considerations
nodes.summary: Commercial aircraft development and production require complex supplier coordination and skilled labor, with costly technological challenges such as 787 rework. New models and derivatives face schedule, production, certification, and heightened regulatory risks following the 737 MAX accidents. Delivery, performance, reliability, and profitability may be affected by program accounting, customer/model mix, costs and rates, inflation, capacity investment, learning curves, changes, cost-reduction efforts, regulations, testing, demand, and customer or supplier claims. Despite estimates believed appropriate, technical complexity may drive extra costs, delays, cancellations, or other significant exposure. The text then introduces Defense, Space & Security business environment and trends.

nodes.title: United States Government Defense Environment Overview
nodes.summary: The FY22 U.S. budget request included $715 billion for DoD, $25 billion for NASA and $19 billion for the FAA, but omitted production funding for the F/A-18, P-8 and CH-47F Block II; congressional support and non-U.S. sales opportunities continued amid appropriation uncertainty. The FY22 Defense Authorization Act authorized $25 billion more than requested, while a continuing resolution funded government at FY21 levels through February 18, 2022. Further resolutions could restrict or delay programs, and a shutdown or future budget changes could materially affect company operations and financial results. International defense demand is driven by security challenges and equipment modernization; BDS sees opportunities in Asia, Europe and the Middle East, and non-U.S. customers represented 33% of its year-end 2021 backlog.

It cautions that long-term contracts, varied delivery and milestone schedules, and differing order structures make period results and backlog comparisons unreliable indicators of future performance. It also lists annual deliveries by aircraft model, including new-builds, remanufactures, and modifications, totaling 169 units in 2021, 154 in 2020, and 229 in 2019.

nodes.title: Revenues
nodes.summary: BDS revenue rose $283 million in 2021 versus 2020, mainly from KC-46A Tanker orders for 27 aircraft and lower charges, partly offset by lower rotorcraft, Commercial Crew, and VC-25B revenue. Catch-up adjustments were $56 million less unfavorable, largely due to lower charges. Revenue rose $162 million in 2020 versus 2019, as growth in fighter aircraft, Space Launch System, B-52 upgrades, proprietary programs, and MQ-25 was partly offset by lower missile-defense volume and catch-up adjustments $312 million more unfavorable, primarily due to KC-46A charges.

nodes.title: Earnings From Operations
nodes.summary: BDS operating earnings rose $5 million in 2021 versus 2020 as less unfavorable contract catch-up adjustments—improving $219 million, largely from lower KC-46A and other development charges—were offset by lower rotorcraft volume and mix and reduced ULA equity earnings. 2021 charges included reach-forward losses of $402 million on KC-46A, $185 million on Commercial Crew, and $318 million on VC-25B, driven by disruption, evolving requirements, delays, and supplier issues. In 2020, earnings fell $1.076 billion versus 2019, mainly due to $828 million higher unfavorable catch-up adjustments, including KC-46A and VC-25B losses, partly offset by lower Commercial Crew charges, volume increases, and other factors; property-sale gains also declined. Equity-method investment income was $53 million, $141 million, and $128 million in 2021, 2020, and 2019, primarily from ULA and non-U.S. joint ventures.

nodes.title: Backlog
nodes.summary:
Backlog
Total backlog of $59,828 million at December 31, 2021 was $1,019 million lower than December 31, 2020 due to the timing of awards and revenue recognized.

nodes.title: Additional Considerations
nodes.summary: BDS development programs face technical, cost and schedule risks: cost-type contracts may lose fees or be canceled, while fixed-price programs—including several named aircraft, spacecraft and satellite programs—may incur or add reach-forward losses, charges, delays, termination exposure, or lost in-orbit incentives. BGS covers aviation aftermarket and government services. COVID-19 hurt commercial services; long-term demand is supported by fleet growth, analytics, outsourced spares management and aging aircraft, while government demand is stable but U.S. spending uncertainty may delay work. Competition creates pricing pressure, and global market access matters. In 2021, BGS revenue rose to $16.328 billion and operating earnings to $2.017 billion, with a 12.4% margin, as commercial and government volumes increased; commercial activity remained below pre-pandemic levels, and pandemic-related revenue impacts are expected to persist.

nodes.title: Global Services Market and 2021 Results
nodes.summary: The page describes aerospace services markets, including commercial aftermarket demand, pandemic impacts, airline efficiency and inventory trends, and stable government-services demand shaped by fleet growth, aging aircraft, and U.S. spending uncertainty. It notes intense domestic and international competition, pricing pressure, and the importance of global market access. For 2021, Global Services reported $16.328 billion in revenue (26% of company revenue), $2.017 billion in operating earnings, and a 12.4% operating margin.

nodes.title: Revenues
nodes.summary: BGS revenue rose $785 million in 2021 as commercial and government services volume improved, though commercial activity remained below pre-pandemic levels and COVID-19 effects are expected to persist; revenue fell $2.925 billion in 2020. Operating earnings increased $1.567 billion in 2021, reflecting recovery and prior-year pandemic-related charges, partly offset by a $220 million inventory write-down and lower contract catch-up benefits; earnings fell $2.247 billion in 2020. Backlog declined 1% to $20.496 billion. Boeing Capital’s portfolio totaled $1.734 billion, with sub-investment-grade and aircraft-type concentration; it provided $14 million financing in 2020 and none in 2021, while expecting alternative funding. Aircraft parking, retirement, and possible further valuation declines pose risks to deliveries, customer payments, financing opportunities, and portfolio values.

nodes.title: BGS Results, Backlog, and Boeing Capital Trends
nodes.summary: BGS revenue and operating earnings fell in 2020 amid COVID-19 impacts, then earnings rose in 2021 due to prior-year charges and higher commercial services volume, partly offset by a contract inventory write-down; the text details charges and contract catch-up adjustments. BGS backlog declined 1% in 2021, mainly as prior-year awards generated revenue. Boeing Capital’s portfolio, below-investment-grade customer exposure, aircraft concentration, financing activity, and expected financing availability are described. Parked aircraft levels, expected retirements, and potential declines in aircraft values affect deliveries, customer payments, financing opportunities, and portfolio risk.

nodes.title: BCC Revenues and Operating Results
nodes.summary: The page reports BCC results for 2019–2021: revenues of $272 million, $244 million, and $261 million; operating earnings of $28 million, $63 million, and $106 million; and margins of 11%, 24%, and 39%, respectively. Revenues chiefly comprise equipment operating-lease income, financing-receivable and note interest, and other income. Revenue growth in 2020 and 2021 primarily reflected asset re-lease gains, partly offset by portfolio run-off. Operating earnings are stated after interest, loss provisions or recoveries, impairments, leased-equipment depreciation, and other expenses; increases in 2020 and 2021 mainly reflected higher revenues and lower impairment and interest expenses, with lower loss provisions also contributing in 2021.

nodes.title: Financial Position
Financial Position (intro)
nodes.summary: BCC’s 2021 financial position shows a smaller customer-financing portfolio and total assets than in 2020, mainly due to $241 million in note payoffs and portfolio run-off; the table also reports liabilities, equity, and debt-to-equity ratios. It notes intercompany guarantees and subsidies. The cash-flow table covers 2019–2021. Operating cash use fell sharply in 2021 versus 2020, driven by a lower net loss and improved working-capital changes; discussion covers non-cash charges, aircraft inventory and delivery trends, 737 MAX compensation and DOJ payments, tax refunds, advances and progress billings, and expected cash-flow pressures. The 2020 decline versus 2019 reflects net losses, inventory growth, write-downs, credit-loss allowances, lower payables and supplier financing, and customer compensation.

nodes.title: Liquidity, Capital Resources, and Cash Flows
nodes.summary: The page presents a cash flow summary in millions for 2021, 2020, and 2019, listing net loss, non-cash items, changes in assets and liabilities, operating, investing, and financing cash flows, foreign exchange effects, and changes in cash including restricted cash, with beginning- and end-of-year balances.

nodes.title: Operating Activities
nodes.summary: Operating cash use was $3.4 billion in 2021, down from $18.4 billion in 2020, versus $2.4 billion in 2019. The 2021 improvement reflected lower net loss and better asset/liability changes; non-cash items included a $3.5 billion 787 reach-forward loss, shares issued for 401(k) contributions, and one-time employee stock grants. Inventory growth slowed as 787 and 777X buildup was partly offset by lower 737 MAX inventory. The text details 737 MAX customer compensation and DOJ-related payments, $1.7 billion in tax refunds, and advances shifting from $1.1 billion used in 2020 to $2.5 billion provided in 2021. The 2020 decline versus 2019 reflected net loss, inventory increases, supplier-payable reductions, and other asset/liability changes, partly offset by non-cash items including a $6.5 billion 777X loss; 2019 included a $7.4 billion favorable customer-consideration liability change. Supply-chain financing payables fell in 2021 and 2020 and rose in 2019, driven by purchasing, payment terms, and program use, but were not material to liquidity. Cash-flow pressure was expected to continue until 787 deliveries resumed and 737 MAX deliveries ramped up.

nodes.title: Investing Activities
nodes.summary: Investing activities provided $9.3 billion in cash in 2021, versus using $18.4 billion in 2020 and $1.5 billion in 2019. The 2021 improvement primarily reflected $27.1 billion in higher net investment proceeds; the 2020 deterioration primarily reflected $17.4 billion in higher net investment contributions. Net investment proceeds were $9.8 billion in 2021 and $0.1 billion in 2019, while 2020 saw $17.3 billion in net contributions. Capital expenditures were $1.0 billion, $1.3 billion, and $1.8 billion in 2021, 2020, and 2019, respectively. Spending was reduced in 2021 and 2020 to manage liquidity during the pandemic and 737 MAX grounding, and is expected to rise in 2022.

nodes.title: Financing Activities
nodes.summary: Financing activities used $5.6 billion in 2021, versus providing $35.0 billion in 2020 and $5.7 billion in 2019. Year-over-year changes mainly reflect shifts between net debt repayments and borrowings, as well as reduced share repurchases and dividends after the March 2020 dividend suspension. Net debt repayments were $5.6 billion in 2021, including $13.8 billion of term-loan repayments partly offset by $9.8 billion of senior notes; net borrowings were $36.3 billion in 2020 and $13.2 billion in 2019, largely from senior notes and term loans. Debt totaled $58.1 billion at year-end 2021 and $63.6 billion in 2020, including short-term debt and BCC balances. No open-market shares were repurchased in 2021 or 2020; 6.9 million shares worth $2.7 billion were repurchased in 2019, and the program was suspended in April 2019 before its authorization was terminated in March 2020. Employee tax withholdings transferred 0.3 million, 0.6 million, and 0.6 million shares in 2021, 2020, and 2019. Dividends were zero in 2021, versus $1.2 billion in 2020 and $4.6 billion in 2019.

nodes.title: Capital Resources
nodes.summary: COVID-19, 787 production problems and rework, and lingering 737 MAX impacts are pressuring liquidity and operations, prompting substantial liquidity-preservation actions. The text summarizes contractual obligations as of December 31, 2021, including debt, interest, pension and postretirement costs, purchase commitments, and 737 MAX customer concessions. Funding is expected from cash, investments, operating cash flow, and capital markets; the company held $8.1 billion cash, $8.2 billion short-term investments, and $14.7 billion unused revolving credit capacity, with specified expirations. Debt has risen, though $13.8 billion of term-loan borrowings was repaid in 2021. Credit ratings were downgraded in 2020 and unchanged in 2021; market, business, and rating deterioration could raise borrowing costs or restrict access to financing. Future borrowing may affect ratings and is subject to covenants; the company was compliant and retained substantial borrowing capacity.

nodes.title: Pension and Other Postretirement Benefits
nodes.summary: The text explains pension and postretirement funding estimates, noting GAAP pension underfunding of $7.8 billion in 2021 versus $13.7 billion in 2020, full funding under ERISA in 2021, no expected significant 2022 contributions, and possible higher future contributions. It describes a $3 billion stock contribution to pensions in 2020 and ongoing stock funding of 401(k) contributions, managed by an independent fiduciary. It defines purchase obligations, details recorded and unrecorded commitments—especially inventory contracts, supplier arrangements, customer support, and estimated escalation costs—and describes international industrial participation commitments, possible penalties, and none incurred in 2021.

nodes.title: Purchase Obligations
nodes.summary: Pension funding requirements follow ERISA minimums, with possible discretionary contributions; other postretirement estimates reflect benefit payments and trust contributions. GAAP pension underfunding was $7.8 billion in 2021 versus $13.7 billion in 2020, while ERISA funding exceeded 100% in 2021; significant 2022 contributions are not expected, though future contributions may rise. The company contributed $3 billion of stock to its pension fund in 2020 and uses stock for ongoing 401(k) contributions, managed and liquidated by an independent fiduciary, to conserve cash. Purchase obligations include legally binding goods and services contracts, both recorded and unrecorded; unrecorded commitments cover inventory, tooling, utilities, capital equipment, customer financing equipment, and other production needs. Inventory contracts are the largest, often involve long lead times and supplier readiness, and are partly customer-supported; estimates include applicable escalation adjustments. Recorded obligations mainly include payables and accrued liabilities. Industrial participation agreements support non-U.S. customers through local work, orders, bidding opportunities, technology transfers, or other assistance; penalties may apply, but none were incurred in 2021. Agreements totaled $25.5 billion through 2034, with related purchase orders included in obligations and awarded only to capable, competitive suppliers.

nodes.title: Off-Balance Sheet Arrangements
nodes.summary: The company has off-balance-sheet arrangements, including guarantees, discussed in Note 14. At December 31, 2021, commercial commitments totaled $16.539 billion: $3.634 billion in standby letters of credit and surety bonds and $12.905 billion in aircraft financing commitments, with amounts scheduled across maturity periods. Aircraft financing commitments cover aircraft orders, options, sales campaigns, and refinancing; customer commitments rose from $11.5 billion in 2020, mainly due to new commitments. The company expects third-party financing to limit funding needs, though greater funding cannot be ruled out (Note 13). Contingent obligations include legal proceedings and investigations (Note 21) and environmental remediation, for which a $605 million liability was recorded (Note 13). Non-GAAP core operating earnings, margin, and EPS supplement GAAP results, exclude the FAS/CAS service-cost adjustment, should not replace GAAP measures, and may differ across companies; investors are urged to review full reports.

BCC’s 2021 position reflects a smaller financing portfolio and asset base after note payoffs and run-off; reported measures include liabilities, equity, leverage, guarantees, subsidies, and three-year cash flows. The section reviews operating cash use and its drivers, investing and financing flows, debt, dividends, share repurchases, capital spending, liquidity resources, obligations, credit risks, and funding plans. It also covers pension and postretirement funding, supplier and industrial-participation commitments, off-balance-sheet guarantees and aircraft financing, contingencies, and the role and limitations of non-GAAP measures.

nodes.title: Commercial Commitments and Contingent Obligations
nodes.summary: The page notes $25.5 billion in purchase obligations through 2034, including industrial participation orders subject to supplier capability and competitiveness, and refers to off-balance-sheet guarantees. It summarizes $16.5 billion of commercial commitments at year-end 2021, including standby letters of credit, surety bonds, and $12.9 billion in aircraft financing commitments. Financing commitments increased from $11.5 billion in 2020; significant funding is not expected, though it cannot be assured. Contingent obligations include legal matters and environmental remediation, for which a $605 million liability was recorded.

nodes.title: Core Operating Earnings, Core Operating Margin and Core Earnings Per Share
nodes.summary: The text explains Boeing’s non-GAAP core operating earnings, margin and EPS, their exclusions and limitations, and differences between GAAP and CAS pension accounting and allocation. It reports 2019–2021 pension FAS/CAS adjustment and non-operating pension benefit amounts and explains year-over-year drivers. It directs readers to further pension disclosures and says management uses these measures to assess and forecast underlying performance, believing they offer insight into costs driven by market factors or not allocable to U.S. government contracts.

nodes.title: Reconciliation of GAAP Measures to Non-GAAP Measures
nodes.summary: The text reconciles 2019–2021 GAAP operating losses, margins and diluted loss per share to non-GAAP core measures, including pension and postretirement adjustments, taxes and share counts, with explanatory footnotes. It then describes critical accounting policies: long-term contract accounting, the judgment and assumptions involved in estimating sales, costs and profit, quarterly revisions and their effects—including catch-up losses and sensitivity to margin estimates—and the risks of future losses. It also explains program accounting and its reliance on dependable estimates of production quantities, revenue, costs and margins.

nodes.title: Accounting for Long-term Contracts
nodes.summary: The text describes accounting policies for long-term contracts and program accounting. Most BDS and some BGS contracts are single performance obligations; revenue and profit rely on estimates of contract sales and costs, affected by pricing terms, options, performance incentives, regulations, inflation, technical and schedule risks, supplier performance, business volume, COVID-19, asset use, and labor agreements. Estimates are reviewed quarterly, with changes producing cumulative catch-ups or immediate reach-forward losses. Unfavorable catch-ups increased operating losses by $880 million in 2021, $942 million in 2020, and $111 million in 2019; 2021 impacts mainly involved KC-46A, VC-25B, and Commercial Crew fixed-price development programs, with continuing risk. Different assumptions could materially alter earnings; a 1% margin change on profitable long-term contracts would have changed 2021 pretax income by about $300 million. Program accounting requires reliable estimates of revenue, costs, and margins for a defined production quantity that can be reasonably estimated.

nodes.title: Program Accounting
nodes.summary: The text explains Boeing’s critical accounting estimates for long-term contracts and program accounting: revenue, costs, margins and production quantities rely on quarterly-reviewed assumptions, with estimate changes causing catch-up adjustments or immediate losses; 2021–2019 unfavorable contract adjustments and sensitivity to a 1% margin change are quantified. It details program-estimation factors and risks, near-break-even or zero margins on several aircraft programs, and specific 777X delays, its 2020 $6.5 billion loss and potential further losses, plus the 787 delivery pause, 2021 $3.5 billion loss, recovery assumptions and risk of additional material losses.

nodes.title: Goodwill Impairments
nodes.summary: Goodwill is assessed through qualitative screening or quantitative comparison of reporting-unit carrying and fair values; any shortfall, limited to goodwill’s carrying amount, is impairment. Fair values use discounted cash flows and market comparables, with forecasts based on sales, costs, working capital, orders, production, deliveries, supplier and labor contracts, and market conditions, discounted using market capitalization and a control premium. Forecast, discount-rate, and stock-price changes can affect impairment. The April 1, 2021 assessment found no impairment, and each unit’s fair value substantially exceeded carrying value at December 31, 2021, though future changes could trigger charges.

nodes.title: Pension Plans
nodes.summary: Many employees have defined benefit pension benefits, though most nonunion and many union employees moved to company-funded defined contribution plans in 2016, with additional union employees transitioning in 2019. Annual pension measurements depend on assumptions such as discount and asset-return rates, and changes can affect expenses, obligations, and shareholders’ equity. A 25-basis-point discount-rate change alters the projected obligation by −$2.24 billion or +$2.53 billion, with no significant pension-cost impact; the same change in expected asset returns would change 2021 pension cost by ∓$155 million. Note 16 provides three years of assumptions.

nodes.title: Deferred Income Taxes – Valuation Allowance
nodes.summary: The Company reviews deferred tax asset recoverability quarterly, weighing evidence and, due to recent losses, excluding projected earnings. At year-end 2021, it reported $11.258 billion in deferred tax assets, $8.976 billion in liabilities, and a $2.423 billion valuation allowance, mainly for pension-related assets reversing beyond liability reversals; the allowance fell $671 million during the year. Further allowances may affect earnings or comprehensive income. Market-risk disclosures describe limited interest-rate exposure after repaying $13.8 billion in floating-rate debt, and foreign-currency and commodity hedging: hypothetical 10% market moves would change unrealized losses by $241 million and $46 million, respectively, largely offset by underlying transactions. See Note 4 for tax details.

nodes.title: Market Risk Disclosures
nodes.summary: The page discusses interest rate and foreign currency exchange rate risks. Interest rate exposure arises from fixed- and floating-rate debt and customer financing assets and liabilities; fixed-rate debt is not considered materially risky, the $13.8 billion floating-rate loan was repaid in 2021, and customer financing has historically seen no material rate-related gains or losses. Foreign currency risk on customer receipts and supplier payments is hedged with forward contracts. A 10% exchange-rate change would alter unrealized contract losses by $241 million, but corresponding changes in hedged transactions offset them, leaving no material combined market risk.

nodes.title: Commodity Price Risk
nodes.summary: The text explains commodity price risk: commodity swaps and purchase contracts hedge market-price changes in production inputs; at December 31, 2021, a 10% price change would shift derivative unrealized losses by $46 million, offset by remeasurement gains or losses on hedged transactions, leaving no material combined market risk. It then provides the financial statements and supplementary data index, listing consolidated statements, business segment data, Notes 1–22 covering accounting policies and financial topics, and independent auditor reports, with page references.

Reports Boeing’s 2019–2021 GAAP and non-GAAP results, revenues, losses, margins, EPS, expenses, R&D, segment performance, deliveries, orders, and backlog, with explanations of year-over-year drivers and program developments across Commercial Airplanes, Defense, Space & Security, Global Services, and Boeing Capital. Covers industry, pandemic, trade, geopolitical, government-budget, competition, recovery, and operational risks; financing, cash flows, commitments, contingencies, pensions, and liquidity; non-GAAP reconciliations; critical contract and program accounting estimates, goodwill, taxes, pensions, and market risks; and indexes the financial statements, notes, and auditor reports.

It then presents Item 7’s management discussion: Boeing’s businesses and strategy; pandemic, production, market, supplier, and funding conditions and outlook; and consolidated operating results. It reviews 2019–2021 GAAP and non-GAAP performance, segment results, deliveries, orders and backlog, risks, cash flows, financing, commitments, contingencies, liquidity, accounting estimates, goodwill, taxes, pensions, market risks, and related financial statements and auditor reports.

title: The Boeing Company and Subsidiaries Consolidated Statements of Operations
key_items: Loss from operations; Loss before income taxes; Diluted loss per share
summary: Boeing’s consolidated statements of operations present 2021, 2020, and 2019 figures in millions of dollars, except per-share data. They report product and service sales, total revenues, costs and expenses, operating investment income or loss, administrative and research expenses, disposition gains, operating and pretax losses, other income, interest and debt expense, tax benefits, net losses, losses attributable to noncontrolling interests and Boeing shareholders, and basic and diluted loss per share. The statements refer readers to notes on pages 64–123.

title: The Boeing Company and Subsidiaries Consolidated Statements of Comprehensive Income
summary: Consolidated statements of comprehensive income for Boeing for 2021, 2020, and 2019 report net losses and other comprehensive income or loss, net of tax. Items include currency translation, investment gains, derivative instrument gains and reclassifications, and defined-benefit pension and postretirement benefit actuarial changes, amortization, settlements, prior-service items, and equity-method effects. The statements give total other comprehensive income or loss, amounts related to noncontrolling interests, and comprehensive income or loss attributable to Boeing shareholders, with a reference to financial statement notes.

title: The Boeing Company and Subsidiaries Consolidated Statements of Financial Position
key_items: Assets; Total liabilities; Total shareholders’ deficit
summary: A comparative Boeing consolidated statement of financial position for 2021 and 2020, in millions of dollars, lists assets (current and noncurrent), liabilities (current and long-term), and shareholders’ equity or deficit, including common-stock details, treasury stock, retained earnings, accumulated other comprehensive loss, and noncontrolling interests. It reports total assets, total liabilities, and total liabilities and equity for each year and refers readers to the notes to the consolidated financial statements.

title: The Boeing Company and Subsidiaries Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows
summary: A Boeing consolidated statement of cash flows for 2019–2021, in millions of dollars, reports net losses and operating cash-flow adjustments, including noncash items and changes in assets and liabilities; net cash used in operating activities; investing cash flows from property, acquisitions, and investments; financing cash flows from borrowing, repayments, equity, repurchases, dividends, and other items; foreign-exchange effects; and beginning, ending, restricted, and unrestricted cash balances. It refers readers to the financial-statement notes.
