nodes.title: The Boeing Company and Subsidiaries Consolidated Statements of Equity (intro)
nodes.summary: The excerpt presents Boeing’s consolidated statements of equity for 2019–2021, including changes in share capital, paid-in capital, treasury shares, retained earnings, accumulated other comprehensive loss, noncontrolling interests, and total equity. It also summarizes segment revenues and operating results, unallocated items, interest, taxes, net losses and losses attributable to Boeing shareholders for 2019–2021, and refers readers to the financial-statement notes and Note 22 for further segment results.

nodes.title: Note 1 – Summary of Significant Accounting Policies Principles of Consolidation and Basis of Presentation
nodes.summary: Boeing management prepared the consolidated financial statements, which include all majority-owned subsidiaries and variable interest entities requiring consolidation, with significant intercompany accounts and transactions eliminated. Boeing operates four reportable segments: Commercial Airplanes, Defense, Space & Security, Global Services, and Boeing Capital.

nodes.title: Liquidity Matters
nodes.summary: The text describes COVID-19, 787 production problems and 737 MAX impacts on demand, deliveries, revenue and cash flow, with recovery expected to take years. It details 2021 operating cash use, debt issuance and repayment, cash, debt, upcoming maturities, credit capacity and ratings, and supply-chain financing. Liquidity measures include suspending buybacks and dividends, cost and workforce reductions, stock-based compensation, customer and supplier coordination, and tax refunds; management expects to fund operations for the foreseeable future. It also explains estimation uncertainty, the operating-cycle policy, and commercial aircraft revenue allocation, point-in-time recognition, bill-and-hold conditions and program accounting.

nodes.title: COVID-19 Response, Estimates, and Operating Cycle
nodes.summary: The company describes cash-preservation measures, including production and workforce reductions, stock in lieu of 401(k) contributions and merit increases, lower discretionary spending, and efforts with customers and suppliers to accelerate receipts. U.S. DoD liquidity initiatives and CARES Act tax refunds of $1.7 billion supported cash. The company expects to fund operations for the foreseeable future based on current estimates and liquidity access. It notes COVID-19 uncertainty may cause actual results to differ from financial estimates. For certain current assets and liabilities, its operating cycle is the contract or program duration, generally over one year.

nodes.title: Revenue and Related Cost Recognition
nodes.summary: Describes revenue and cost recognition across commercial aircraft, long-term defense and government contracts, spare parts, services, concessions, contract assets and liabilities, financial services, and reinsurance. It explains transaction-price allocation, performance obligations, point-in-time versus over-time recognition, variable consideration, payment terms, financing-component treatment, cost and profit estimation, cumulative catch-up adjustments and loss provisions, including historical adjustments and major program losses. It also covers financing-receivable collectability, non-accrual treatment, lease income, residual-value estimates, operating-lease depreciation, and reinsurance revenues and costs.

nodes.title: Fleet Support
nodes.summary: Fleet support covers training, field and engineering assistance, technical documentation, and consulting before delivery and throughout aircraft service; post-delivery work includes maintenance and operational issue support, manual and data updates, and fleet-wide service bulletins, with costs expensed as incurred. Research and development costs are generally expensed, except qualifying customer-contract costs recognized alongside revenue; certain customer funding offsets expense, and annual bid/proposal costs are reported. Share-based compensation is measured at grant-date fair value for share-settled awards and reporting-date fair value for cash-settled or potentially cash-settled awards, net of forfeitures, and recognized over the service period. Income taxes reflect applicable jurisdictions and tax-rate changes; timing differences create deferred taxes, and significant judgment applies to uncertain tax positions, interest and penalties, and deferred-tax-asset recoverability and valuation allowances.

nodes.title: Fleet Support, R&D, Compensation, and Taxes
nodes.summary: Fleet support spans pre-delivery training and technical assistance through ongoing operational support; its costs are expensed as incurred. R&D costs are generally expensed, except qualifying customer-contract costs recognized alongside revenue; qualifying customer funding offsets R&D expense, which included specified bid and proposal costs for 2019–2021. Share-based awards are measured at grant-date fair value if share-settled or reporting-date fair value if cash-settled, net of estimated forfeitures, and expensed over the service period. Income tax accounting covers current and deferred taxes, timing differences, judgment and uncertain tax positions, related interest and penalties, and valuation allowances for deferred tax assets, with estimate changes recorded when determined.

nodes.title: Benefit Plans, Environmental Liabilities, and Cash Policies
nodes.summary: The page explains pension and other retiree benefits, plan transitions, actuarial cost assumptions, accounting for service costs and actuarial gains or losses, and funded-status reporting. It describes when postemployment benefit liabilities are recognized. It outlines environmental remediation assessment, accrual, estimation, discounting, and probable recoveries. Cash equivalents are highly liquid instruments with original maturities of three months or less; eligible balances are aggregated by bank, and negative balances are reclassified to accounts payable ($47 in 2021; $74 in 2020).

nodes.title: Inventories
nodes.summary: Inventories include direct engineering, production, tooling, applicable overhead, and certain reengineering costs, subject to net realizable value; abnormal or ineligible fixed costs are expensed, and some costs relate to long-term cycles. Commercial aircraft inventory includes deferred early-production costs, expected to be recovered across program deliveries, and supplier advances amortized as parts arrive. Quarterly reviews estimate contract and program completion costs and record losses when costs exceed revenues. Used aircraft and general materials are carried at cost up to net realizable value; spare parts at the lower of average cost or net realizable value, with impaired or obsolete stock expensed. Airline early issue sales consideration is recorded in inventory and reduces revenue upon delivery; unrecoverable amounts are written off.

nodes.title: Precontract Costs
nodes.summary: The company may incur costs beyond existing contract requirements. Costs deemed probably recoverable through future orders are capitalized as precontract costs and included in Inventories; start-up costs are expensed as incurred. Capitalized costs are written off if future orders do not materialize or recovery is no longer considered probable.

nodes.title: Property, Plant and Equipment
nodes.summary: Property and equipment are recorded at cost, including construction-period interest, less depreciation; buildings and improvements use 150% declining balance over 10–40 years, and machinery uses sum-of-the-years’ digits over 4–20 years. Internal-use software and software-as-a-service costs are capitalized in Other assets and amortized straight-line over five years or the hosting term (typically up to ten years). Useful lives are periodically reviewed. Assets held for sale are measured at the lower of cost or fair value less selling costs; held-for-use assets are tested for impairment when indicators arise, with losses measured against fair value if undiscounted cash flows cannot recover carrying value. Lease classification is assessed at inception. Operating lease assets and liabilities are recognized at commencement using the present value of payments and an estimated incremental borrowing rate; variable costs are expensed, reasonably certain extension or termination options are included, and expense is straight-line. Finance lease assets and liabilities are reported in property and equipment and debt, respectively. Real-property lease and non-lease components are combined as one lease component.

nodes.title: Asset Retirement Obligations
nodes.summary: The company records known asset retirement obligations when fair value can be reasonably estimated, including asbestos removal, decommissioning, and lease restoration; recorded amounts are immaterial. Known conditional obligations are unrecorded when timing or settlement methods are insufficiently clear, and will be recognized once estimable. Potential undiscovered obligations, such as unknown asbestos, are also excluded from the financial statements.

nodes.title: Goodwill and Other Acquired Intangibles
nodes.summary: Goodwill and indefinite-lived acquired intangibles are not amortized and are tested annually on April 1 and when impairment indicators arise. Goodwill testing uses a qualitative assessment or compares net-asset carrying value with operations’ fair value; impairment is the shortfall, capped at goodwill. Indefinite-lived brand, trade name, and acquired IPR&D are tested against discounted cash flows; completed IPR&D becomes finite-lived and is amortized. Finite-lived assets are straight-line amortized over specified ranges: technology 4–14 years, know-how 6–30, customer base 3–17, distribution rights 3–27, and other 1–32. When impairment indicators arise, recoverability is assessed using undiscounted cash flows, with impairment measured as carrying value above fair value.

nodes.title: Investments
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting policies for investments, derivatives, credit-loss allowances, and aircraft commitments. Time deposits are carried at cost; debt and equity investments are accounted for using fair-value, equity, or adjusted-cost methods, with impairment reviews and gains classified by operating or non-operating purpose. Derivatives are measured at fair value; cash-flow hedge gains and losses are deferred and later recognized in earnings, while non-designated instruments affect earnings immediately. Credit allowances are reviewed quarterly using customer and receivable risk factors. Aircraft trade-in and contingent repurchase commitments, their conditions, and their infrequent conversion are also described.

nodes.title: Investment Income, Derivatives, and Credit Loss Allowances
key_items: Allowances for Losses on Certain Financial Assets
nodes.summary: Investment income and losses are classified as operating or non-operating based on strategic integration, with related earnings, dividends, impairments, and disposition gains or losses reported in designated statement categories. Derivatives are measured at fair value; cash-flow hedge gains and losses are initially recorded in comprehensive income and later reclassified to earnings, while non-designated derivatives—including aluminum purchase and sale agreements—are recognized in earnings as fair values change. Credit-loss allowances cover receivables and other financial assets, are reviewed quarterly using credit, aging, loss-rate, and collateral factors, and rely on internal customer ratings informed by public and customer-provided information, comparable to agency ratings.

nodes.title: Aircraft Valuation
nodes.summary: The text explains valuation and accounting for aircraft trade-in and contingent repurchase commitments, including revenue adjustments, cost charges, accrued-liability estimates, market-based valuation methods, and treatment of acquired aircraft as inventory or leased customer-financing assets. It describes customer financing categories, collateral-based fair-value assessments, and impairment reviews for leased or sale/re-lease assets, including cash-flow assumptions and loss measurement. It also outlines the allowance for customer-financing receivables, its key credit and collateral factors, customer agreements permitting recovery from other assets, quarterly reviews, and uncertainty in estimates.

nodes.title: Warranties
nodes.summary: The text explains warranty coverage across commercial and defense segments, standard periods and covered items, accounting for routine and major-issue costs, and performance guarantees and supplier reimbursements recorded at aircraft delivery. It describes when supplier-penalty accruals are recognized and how guarantee liabilities, including credit guarantees, are measured. It also presents goodwill balances and adjustments by business segment for 2019–2021.

nodes.title: Supplier Penalties and Guarantees
nodes.summary: Performance warranties cover major warranty issues and guarantees to commercial aircraft customers for missed performance targets; estimated costs and liabilities reflect expected operations, remedies, and settlements. Customer payments reduce revenue at aircraft delivery, while supplier recoveries are included in inventories and reduce product costs; both are included in program estimates at completion. Supplier penalties are accrued when probable and estimable. Guarantee liabilities reflect fair value, with credit-guarantee expected loss based on default rates, guarantee amounts, and expected recoveries; contingent-loss liabilities are recognized at inception and adjusted quarterly.

nodes.title: Note 2 – Goodwill and Acquired Intangibles
nodes.summary: The note details goodwill balances and adjustments by business segment from 2019 through 2021. It reports indefinite-lived trade-name assets of $197 and in-process research and development of $202 at both 2021 and 2020 year-ends, plus a 2019 $293 impairment from retiring the Aviall brand. It lists 2021 and 2020 gross carrying amounts and accumulated amortization for acquired finite-lived intangibles, notes a 2020 $178 distribution-rights impairment, gives amortization expense of $284 in 2021 and $317 in 2020, and estimates expense of $245, $236, $221, $195, and $192 for 2022–2026, respectively.

nodes.title: Note 3 – Earnings Per Share
nodes.summary: The note explains that basic and diluted EPS use the two-class method, allocating undistributed earnings between common shares and participating securities, which share equal rights. It gives the EPS formulas and 2019–2021 net losses, participating-security allocations, weighted-average share counts, and basic and diluted loss per share. Diluted calculations may include stock options, restricted stock units, performance-based units, and performance awards; participating securities include certain deferred-compensation instruments. Potential shares excluded as antidilutive totaled 2.6 million, 1.6 million, and 4.1 million in 2021, 2020, and 2019. A table also lists future potential dilutive shares by award type that were excluded because they were antidilutive or performance conditions were unmet.

nodes.title: Note 4 – Income Taxes
nodes.summary: Notes 4–6 report income tax benefits/expenses and cash tax payments for 2019–2021; statutory-rate reconciliations and effects of the CARES Act, share-based tax benefits, audit settlements, and foreign-derived income deductions. They detail deferred tax assets/liabilities, carryover expirations, valuation allowances and their changes, loss-related recoverability judgments, reinvested foreign earnings, tax interest and penalties, unrecognized tax benefits, and audit status. Note 5 presents accounts receivable by category, net of allowances. Note 6 reconciles expected-credit-loss allowances for receivables, unbilled receivables, customer financing, and other assets for 2020–2021.

nodes.title: Tax Audits, Receivables and Credit-Loss Allowances
key_items: Note 6 – Allowances for Losses on Financial Assets
nodes.summary: The page reports that federal tax audits before 2018 are settled; the IRS is auditing 2018–2020, and other jurisdictions may examine 2008–2020, with provisions considered adequate. Note 5 details 2021 and 2020 accounts receivable by category, valuation allowances, and total balances, including definitions of U.S. government contract exclusions. Note 6 presents 2020–2021 allowance rollforwards for accounts receivable, unbilled receivables, customer financing, other current assets, and other assets, showing estimates, write-offs, recoveries, and ending balances.

nodes.title: Note 7 – Inventories
nodes.summary: Note 7 reports inventories at December 31, 2021 and 2020: long-term contracts in progress ($872 million and $823 million), commercial aircraft programs ($68,106 million and $70,153 million), and commercial spare parts, used aircraft, general stock materials and other ($9,845 million and $10,739 million), totaling $78,823 million and $81,715 million, respectively. The last category includes capitalized precontract costs of $648 million in 2021 and $733 million in 2020, primarily for KC-46A Tanker and Commercial Crew; see Note 13.

nodes.title: Commercial Aircraft Programs
nodes.summary: Commercial aircraft inventory fell in 2021 as 737 MAX deliveries resumed and a 787 reach-forward loss was recorded, partly offset by 787 production buildup and 777X growth. Inventory included 335 737 MAX and 110 787 aircraft, versus 425 and 80 in 2020. Customer deferrals and cancellations may require remarketing, rate cuts, or accounting-quantity reductions, risking lower earnings and further losses. The text details 737, 777X, and 787 inventory costs and expected recoveries; reports 777X and 787 reach-forward losses of $6.493 billion and $3.460 billion; outlines risks to 777X profitability; and gives early-issue sales consideration balances of $3.290 billion and $2.992 billion.

nodes.title: Note 8 – Contracts with Customers
nodes.summary: Note 8 reports unbilled receivables rising from $7,995 in 2020 to $8,620 in 2021, mainly because BDS and BGS recognized revenue ahead of billings. Advances and progress billings rose from $50,488 to $52,980, driven by customer advances at BDS, BCA and BGS, partly offset by recognized revenue and returned advances at BCA. Revenue recognized from opening advances was $11,336 in 2021 and $10,360 in 2020. A table details unbillable long-term contract assets and claims by year, collection timing and valuation allowance. Commercial-incentive receivables collectible after one year were $131 and $178, respectively; claims receivables are believed earned but involve uncertainty about determination or realization.

nodes.title: Note 9 – Customer Financing
nodes.summary: Note 9 describes customer financing, primarily in the BCC segment, with 1–12-year arrangements that may allow lease extensions, termination, or aircraft purchase. At year-end 2021/2020, net financing receivables were $1,338/$1,322 million, operating lease equipment was $474/$715 million, and total customer financing was $1,812/$2,037 million. It details lease-payment, residual-value, and unearned-income components; uncollectible non-accrual receivables of $378/$380 million backed by sufficient collateral; interest income of $18/$34 million; and no past-due receivables in 2021. Financing balances are also presented by credit rating and origination year. The 2021 loss allowance covered CCC, B, BB, and BBB ratings, using average default rates of 24.2%, 5.5%, 2.6%, and 0.2%, respectively.

nodes.title: Customer Financing Exposure
nodes.summary: The text reports customer financing exposure by aircraft model for 2021 and 2020, including amounts accounted for as operating leases, and notes that operating-lease equipment is mainly large commercial jets. It provides operating-lease asset impairment charges by year and business category, lease income from sales-type/finance and operating leases, and profit recognized at sales-type lease commencement. It also presents 2021 expected cash flows for notes receivable and sales-type/finance and operating leases over five years and thereafter, including total receipts, imputed interest, residual values and totals; unguaranteed residual values for 2021 and 2020; and states that guaranteed residual values in 2021 were insignificant.

nodes.title: Note 10 – Property, Plant and Equipment
nodes.summary: Note 10 reports property, plant and equipment balances at December 31, 2021 and 2020 by category, including gross assets, accumulated depreciation, and net totals. It also gives depreciation expense and capitalized interest for 2021–2019, non-cash PP&E acquisitions in 2021 and 2020, and accounts payable for PP&E purchases in those years.

nodes.title: Investments and Equity Method Investments
nodes.summary: The page reports investment balances at December 31, 2020 and 2021, including equity method investments, time deposits, available-for-sale debt instruments, equity and other investments, and restricted cash equivalents. It notes dividends received, undistributed equity-method earnings, the HorizonX deconsolidation and related gain from Boeing’s strategic partnership, and the purpose of restricted funds. Available-for-sale debt instruments are investment grade, with no credit-loss allowance recorded. A segment table lists equity-method investment balances and ownership percentages, including United Launch Alliance.

nodes.title: Note 12 – Leases
nodes.summary: Note 12 reports operating lease costs of $380 million in 2021 and $360 million in 2020, including variable costs; cash lease payments and noncash additions; year-end right-of-use assets, liabilities, remaining terms and discount rates; five-year and later maturity payments, including imputed interest; and $265 million of uncommenced hangar leases beginning in 2022–2023. Note 13 lists accrued liabilities by category for 2021 and 2020, including compensation, customer concessions, legal agreement liabilities, warranties, taxes, lease liabilities and other items.

nodes.title: 737 MAX Grounding
nodes.summary: Following two fatal accidents in 2019, regulators grounded the 737 MAX and deliveries stopped. The FAA and many international authorities later cleared operations; China issued return-to-service requirements in late 2021, with deliveries expected to resume in 2022 subject to approval and timing risks. Over 185 countries have approved operations, though a few jurisdictions remain grounded. Production is expected to reach 31 aircraft monthly by early 2022, with later increases dependent on demand and supply capacity. Abnormal production costs were $2.567 billion in 2020 and $1.887 billion in 2021; remaining costs are expected to be insignificant and mostly incurred early in 2022. Boeing delivered 245 aircraft in 2021 and held about 335 in inventory at year-end, most expected to be delivered by 2023; customer deferrals, cancellations, remarketing, China delivery delays, or slower ramp-up could affect delivery and production plans. Grounding-related expenses were $328 million in 2019, $416 million in 2020, and $175 million in 2021, covering storage, inventory impairment, pilot training, and software updates. Customer-concessions liabilities fell from $5.537 billion in 2020 to $2.940 billion in 2021. The 2021 balance comprises $2.2 billion contracted ($1.0 billion in reduced delivery payments, $1.0 billion cash, and $0.2 billion other concessions) and $0.7 billion under negotiation; $0.8 billion of cash payments are expected in 2022.

nodes.title: Environmental
nodes.summary: Environmental remediation liabilities were $605 at December 31, 2021, up from $565 in 2020, reflecting payments of $59 and $42, respectively, and estimate increases of $99 and $37. Recorded liabilities represent the best estimate or low end of reasonably possible costs, including up to 30 years of site operation and maintenance. Actual costs may be higher due to regulatory actions, legal changes, unexpected costs, or newly found contamination; some obligations cannot be reasonably estimated. The high-end cost estimate exceeded recorded liabilities by $1,094 in 2021 and $1,095 in 2020.

nodes.title: Product Warranties and Aircraft Commitments
nodes.summary: The page reports 2021 and 2020 product warranty reserve activity and explains the 2020 increase, including charges for 737NG pickle-fork inspections and repairs, revised estimates, and uncertainty about possible additional losses. It also describes aircraft trade-in commitments, how exercise probability is assessed, their terms and 2022–2028 expirations, and contractual totals, estimated net obligations, and related aircraft fair values for 2021 and 2020.

nodes.title: Financial Commitments and Contract Risks
key_items: Standby Letters of Credit and Surety Bonds
nodes.summary: Financing commitments for aircraft and refinancing totaled $12.905 billion in 2021 versus $11.512 billion in 2020, with estimated funding dates provided; all involved customers considered below investment grade, but no loss reserve was deemed necessary given the terms. The company also committed $248 million to joint ventures over six years and had letters of credit and surety-bond liabilities of $3.634 billion in 2021 versus $4.238 billion in 2020. Legacy executive life-insurance obligations had policy values and loans, presented net as an asset. Fixed-price development contracts have incurred loss charges and carry uncertainty and risks of further charges, termination, cancellations, or other significant exposure.

nodes.title: Tanker Contract, Government Costs, and Severance
nodes.summary: The page describes the USAF KC-46A contract, covering four development aircraft and seven authorized production lots totaling 94 aircraft, valued at about $19 billion; it also reports $243 million in capitalized precontract costs and $409 million in potential supplier termination liabilities. Government-incurred costs are subject to audit, disputes, possible reserves, earnings charges, or refunds. Severance liability changes are summarized for 2020–2021; planned departures fell from about 26,000 employees in 2020 to 19,000 in 2021, and the year-end liability mainly covers payments to terminated employees.

nodes.title: Note 14 – Arrangements with Off-Balance Sheet Risk
nodes.summary: Note 14 describes off-balance-sheet risks, primarily guarantees, and presents maximum potential payments, estimated collateral/recourse proceeds, and recorded liabilities for contingent aircraft repurchase commitments and credit guarantees. Repurchase estimates use the lower of contracted price or expected aircraft fair value; credit guarantees cover lessee or debtor defaults, are generally collateralized, and expire through 2036. St. Louis industrial revenue bonds finance recorded property; the company holds the bonds, and related assets and liabilities were each $271 million in 2020 and 2021. Indemnities for certain sold businesses and facilities cover indefinite pre-closing environmental and other claims; potential payments cannot be estimated, so no liability is recorded unless claims are probable and estimable, when included in environmental liabilities.

nodes.title: Note 15 – Debt
nodes.summary: Note 15 details 2021 senior note issuances, repayment of a delayed-draw loan, interest incurred and paid, available revolving credit facilities and covenant compliance. It presents short-term debt and current maturities, debt balances by rate and maturity, allocation between BCC and Boeing, and scheduled debt and lease payments for 2022–2026. Note 16 describes defined-benefit pension plans, employees’ transitions to defined-contribution plans, pension trust funding and investment aims, and retiree health and life insurance benefits, including coverage limits and lifetime coverage for some groups.

nodes.title: Debt Balances and Scheduled Payments
nodes.summary: Lists unsecured debt by interest-rate range and maturity, finance lease obligations, other notes, and total debt for 2021 and 2020. Shows total debt attributable to BCC and Other Boeing, and scheduled debt principal payments and minimum finance lease obligations for 2022–2026.

nodes.title: Note 16 – Postretirement Plans
nodes.summary: The note describes defined-benefit pension transitions to company-funded defined-contribution plans in 2016 and 2019, pension trust funding and investment goals, and retiree health and life-insurance benefits. It explains how pension and other postretirement benefit (OPB) funded status is measured and classified on the balance sheet, including amounts due within 12 months. Tables report 2019–2021 pension and OPB periodic benefit cost components and income-statement presentation. In 2021, a $193 settlement charge and plan remeasurement were recorded; subsequent tables cover 2020–2021 changes in obligations, assets and funded status.

nodes.title: Amounts recognized in statement of financial position at December 31 consist of:
nodes.summary: The text reports pension and other postretirement benefit amounts recognized on the balance sheet at December 31, 2021 and 2020, including asset and liability components and net recognized amounts. It also presents actuarial losses or gains and prior service credits in accumulated other comprehensive loss for both benefit types. Pension plan accumulated benefit obligations were $74.2 million and $80.7 million, respectively; for plans whose obligations exceeded assets, it gives accumulated and projected benefit obligations alongside plan-asset fair values for both years.

nodes.title: Assumptions
nodes.summary: The text lists weighted-average assumptions for benefit obligations and subsequent-year periodic costs for 2021, 2020, and 2019: pension and postretirement discount rates, expected asset returns, compensation growth, and cash-balance interest rates. It explains that discount rates derive from a high-quality Aa-or-better bond yield curve, excluding the highest and lowest 10% of yields, and are applied to projected benefit cash flows. Expected asset returns reflect historical and prospective asset-class performance; costs use that assumption and a five-year moving-average market-related asset value, which was about $4,773 below fair value at December 31, 2021. It also reports health-care trend assumptions: next-year and ultimate rates, with the ultimate rate reached in 2021.

nodes.title: Plan Assets
Investment Strategy
nodes.summary: The text describes pension asset investment objectives, including meeting benefit obligations, liquidity, risk reduction, competitive returns, diversification, and risk management. It explains periodic strategic allocation reviews, liability and funding considerations, de-risking as funding improves, benchmarks, allocation fluctuations, and frequent rebalancing. It lists actual and target allocations for 2021 and 2020 across fixed income, global equity, private equity, real estate and real assets, and hedge funds, and outlines each asset class’s investments and strategies. It also covers managers’ contractual guidelines and permitted derivative uses, derivative exposures in 2021 and 2020, and the company-stock contribution, independent liquidation management, and remaining holdings.

nodes.title: Risk Management
nodes.summary: Pension asset risk management addresses funded status, interest rate, market, counterparty, liquidity, and operational risks. It emphasizes liability matching and diversification across asset classes, strategies, managers, industries or sectors, and holdings. Public-asset manager guidelines are monitored by the custodian, and credit limits apply to counterparties trading over-the-counter derivatives. Valuation controls include reviews of manager and custodian policies, pricing vendors, reconciliations, and periodic security-specific testing.

nodes.title: Fair Value Measurements
nodes.summary: Presents pension plan asset fair values at December 31, 2021 and 2020 by hierarchy Levels 1–3, investment category, and NAV practical expedient, defining each level. Describes valuation methods and inputs for fixed income, pooled funds, derivatives, cash investments, equities, private investments, real estate/assets, REITs, commodities, and hedge funds, including NAV reporting and lag adjustments. Reconciles Level 3 assets for both years, showing gains and losses, purchases and settlements, transfers, ending balances, and unrealized results for assets still held.

nodes.title: OPB Plan Assets
nodes.summary: Most OPB assets are in a 60/40 equity-debt index fund valued at Level 1; its return assumption does not materially affect benefit costs. Pension contributions are not expected to be significant in 2022, with no discretionary contributions planned; $3,000 in common stock was contributed in 2020. The text lists projected pension and postretirement benefit payments for 2022–2031. Certain plans allocate assets after an unapproved change of control or termination to ERISA benefits, postretirement benefit trusts, and potentially the U.S. government. Defined contribution plans, chiefly 401(k)s, had expenses of $1,268, $1,351, and $1,533 in 2021, 2020, and 2019. The 2003 Incentive Stock Plan authorizes various equity and cash awards and 87 million shares; issuances generally use treasury shares, considered sufficient for 2022.

nodes.title: Pension Benefits and Compensation Plans
nodes.summary: The page notes that pension-asset return assumptions have no material effect on benefit cost, and that required or discretionary pension contributions are not expected to be significant in 2022; $3,000 in common stock was contributed in 2020. It lists projected pension and other postretirement benefit payments for 2022–2031. It explains pension-plan termination provisions involving ERISA benefits, postretirement-benefit trusts, and U.S. government claims to certain surplus assets. Defined contribution plan expenses for 2019–2021 are reported. The 2003 Incentive Stock Plan’s eligible participants, award types, 87 million authorized shares, and use of treasury or new shares for settlements are described.

Covers pension investment objectives, allocation and strategies, asset-class holdings, benchmarks, rebalancing, derivatives, company-stock contributions, and risk controls for funded status, markets, counterparties, liquidity, operations, and valuations. Reports 2021 and 2020 asset allocations and fair values by hierarchy, valuation methods, and Level 3 reconciliations. Describes OPB assets, expected contributions and benefit payments, plan termination provisions, defined contribution expenses, and the 2003 Incentive Stock Plan’s awards, share authorization, and settlement practices.

nodes.title: Pension Cash Flows, Termination, and Defined Contributions
nodes.summary: Expected pension asset returns do not materially affect benefit cost. Significant required pension contributions are not expected in 2022, and no discretionary contributions are planned; $3,000 in company stock was contributed in 2020. Estimated pension and other postretirement benefit payments for 2022–2031 are reported, including gross benefits, subsidies, and net benefits. Certain plan terminations following an unapproved change in control prioritize ERISA-required benefits, then fund a trust for postretirement medical and life benefits; the U.S. government may also receive a fair share of surplus assets tied to reimbursed contract contributions. Eligible employees may join defined contribution plans, principally 401(k) plans; expenses were $1,268, $1,351, and $1,533 in 2021, 2020, and 2019.

nodes.title: Share-Based Compensation
nodes.summary: The amended 2003 Incentive Stock Plan authorizes up to 87 million shares for various stock- and cash-based awards to employees, officers, directors, consultants, and contractors. Awards will generally be funded with treasury shares, with new shares used if treasury shares are insufficient; the company expects adequate treasury shares for 2022. Share-based compensation expense is recorded mainly in total costs and expenses and general and administrative expense, with some capitalized in inventory. The text introduces a table of expense and related tax-benefit amounts by year, but provides no figures.

nodes.title: Stock Options
nodes.summary: Describes stock-option grants and terms, including 2021 premium-priced awards to executives and additional retention/achievement awards, vesting, expiration, retirement-related treatment, and valuation assumptions. Earlier options vested over three years and were fully vested by 2017. Reports 2021 option activity and weighted-average exercise prices and remaining life, intrinsic value and tax benefits for options exercised in 2019–2021, unrecognized compensation cost and recognition period, and notes that no options vested in those years.

nodes.title: Restricted Stock Units
nodes.summary: The text describes executive RSU grants in February 2019–2021 and an additional 2021 grant, generally vesting one-for-one on the third anniversary, with prorated or full vesting under specified retirement, layoff, disability, death, age, and service conditions; otherwise, units are forfeited. It also covers a December 2020 one-time employee grant with similar vesting and termination terms, other retention or achievement RSUs, and fair-value measurement using the grant-date average high and low stock prices. A 2021 activity table reports units granted, forfeited, distributed, and outstanding, vested units, unrecognized compensation cost, and remaining amortization periods by RSU category.

nodes.title: Executive Incentive Awards
nodes.summary: Describes PBRSUs tied to three-year relative TSR, with 0%–200% payouts, vesting and stock settlement terms, termination eligibility, 2019–2020 grants, valuation assumptions, expense recognition, and 2021 unit activity and remaining compensation cost. Also covers cash-based Performance Awards tied to three-year financial goals, their payout ranges, payment-form discretion, expense recognition, and maximum payout obligations.

nodes.title: Deferred Compensation and Shareholders’ Equity
nodes.summary: Describes employee and executive deferred compensation plans, their investment options, annual expenses for 2019–2021, and year-end liabilities for 2020–2021. Notes the 2018 authorization of up to $20 billion in share repurchases and its termination in March 2020, authorized common and preferred shares, and the absence of issued preferred stock. A table reports common and treasury share balances and changes from 2019 through 2021.

nodes.title: Accumulated Loss and Cash Flow Hedges
nodes.summary: Reports AOCI component balances and changes for 2019–2021, including currency translation, investment and derivative gains and losses, pension and postretirement benefits, and total amounts net of tax. Footnotes explain pension remeasurements and actuarial-loss amortization. Describes cash flow hedges using foreign currency forwards for forecasted sales and purchases through 2031, and commodity swaps and purchase contracts to manage production input price risk through 2029.

nodes.summary:

nodes.title: Notional Amounts and Fair Values
nodes.summary: The text reports 2021 and 2020 derivative notionals, fair values, balance-sheet classification, and netting, distinguishing designated hedges from derivatives without hedge accounting. It gives hedge gains and losses recognized in other comprehensive income and reclassified from accumulated OCI to earnings, notes insignificant gains or losses on undesignated derivatives, and forecasts $22 million of pretax hedge gains to be reclassified within 12 months. It describes credit-risk settlement and collateral provisions and confirms no collateral was posted. It also explains the three-level fair-value hierarchy, presents recurring fair-value assets and liabilities by level for both years, and describes valuation methods for investments and foreign-exchange and commodity derivatives.

nodes.title: Fair Value Measurements and Hedge Disclosures
nodes.summary: The text reports that $22 million in pre-tax cash-flow hedge gains are expected to be reclassified from accumulated other comprehensive loss into earnings within 12 months. It describes credit-related settlement and collateral provisions for certain foreign-exchange and commodity derivatives; $7 million of such contracts were in a net liability position at December 31, 2021, with no collateral posted. Note 20 explains the three-level fair-value hierarchy and introduces recurring fair-value assets and liabilities, listing money market funds, available-for-sale debt investments, other equity investments, and derivatives.

nodes.title: Liabilities
nodes.summary: The text reports 2021 and 2020 liability fair values by hierarchy level, describes market-based valuation of money market funds, securities, and income-based valuation of foreign currency and commodity derivatives. It presents nonrecurring Level 3 impairment fair values and losses for investments, customer financing assets, other assets, acquired intangibles, and property, plant and equipment. Valuation methods include discounted cash flows and aircraft collateral values from third-party publications, adjusted for individual aircraft condition and attributes. It also details 2021 customer-financing-asset valuation inputs, ranges, median values, and adjustment definitions.

nodes.title: Fair Value Disclosures for Financial Instruments
nodes.summary: Presents carrying amounts and fair values of notes receivable and debt, excluding finance lease obligations, at December 31, 2021 and 2020, with fair value hierarchy levels. Notes receivables are valued using discounted cash flows and comparable loan rates; debt uses market yields, dealer quotes, or discounted cash flows, including Level 3 yields from similar securities. Fair values of indemnifications and financing commitments cannot practicably be estimated. Several cash, deposit, receivable, and payable items are excluded because carrying values approximate fair value; these use Level 2 inputs, except cash, which is Level 1.

nodes.title: Note 21 – Legal Proceedings
nodes.summary: The company faces various product, contract, employment and other lawsuits, claims, and government investigations, which may lead to financial penalties or restrictions; it generally expects no material financial impact except as disclosed. Litigation and investigations relate to the 2018 Lion Air and 2019 Ethiopian Airlines 737 MAX accidents, including an SEC investigation whose outcome may be material; uninsured losses cannot currently be estimated. A proposed shareholder derivative settlement would provide about $237 million and require governance changes, subject to court approval. A 2021 DOJ deferred prosecution agreement requires $2.51 billion in penalties, victim compensation and airline-customer payments, plus compliance reforms; the criminal charge may be dismissed after three years of compliance. The company also disputes Embraer’s challenge to its termination of planned joint ventures; the matter is in arbitration and potential losses cannot be estimated.

nodes.title: Note 22 – Segment and Revenue Information
nodes.summary: The note describes four reportable segments—BCA, BDS, BGS and BCC—their businesses, profit measures and revenue-recognition methods, with other activities classified as unallocated. It reports 2019–2021 revenues by customer geography, U.S. government revenue shares and the proportion of operating assets outside the U.S.; disaggregates BCA, BDS and BGS revenues by customer, contract type and recognition timing; and states equity-method investment income. Backlog was $377.499 billion at year-end 2021, with expected conversion through 2022 and 2025, subject to uncertainty from aircraft production, delivery, entry-into-service and COVID-19 issues.

nodes.title: BGS Revenue, Equity Earnings, and Backlog
nodes.summary: The page reports BGS revenues for 2019–2021 by commercial and government contracts, intersegment revenue, and total segment revenue, plus the shares recognized over time, on fixed-price contracts, and from the U.S. government (including foreign military sales). Equity-method investment income, primarily in BDS, was $40 million in 2021, $86 million in 2020, and $90 million in 2019. It defines backlog and its revenue conversion basis, reports $377.499 billion at year-end 2021, estimates 17% conversion through 2022 and 74% through 2025, and notes timing uncertainty from aircraft production, delivery, certification, and COVID-19 factors.

nodes.title: Unallocated Items and Benefit Expense
key_items: Pension and Other Postretirement Benefit Expense
nodes.summary: Explains unallocated items, eliminations and other, including shared services, BCC guarantees, intersegment sales, and cost-allocation methods, with a table of annual components and amounts for 2019–2021. Describes how pension and postretirement costs are allocated under GAAP and U.S. Government CAS, defines the FAS/CAS service-cost adjustment, and notes that non-service benefit expenses are reported in Other income, net.

nodes.title: Segment Assets and Capital Spending
nodes.summary: Presents segment assets at December 31, 2020 and 2021, noting that unallocated assets mainly include cash, investments, tax assets, capitalized interest, centrally managed assets, and eliminations, and declined primarily due to lower investments. Tables report capital expenditures for 2019–2021 and depreciation and amortization by segment. Unallocated capital spending mainly concerns centrally managed assets; the note explains how centrally managed depreciation is allocated by usage and occupancy, with annual amounts and segment allocations for 2019–2021.

summary: Presents Boeing’s 2019–2021 consolidated equity changes and accounting policies, including consolidation, liquidity, COVID-19 impacts, revenue and cost recognition, estimates, assets, liabilities, taxes, benefits, investments, derivatives, warranties, and financing. Notes and tables cover EPS, receivables, inventory and aircraft program losses, customer financing, leases, debt, pensions, share-based compensation, shareholders’ equity and accumulated other comprehensive loss, fair values, legal proceedings, commitments, environmental matters, and segment revenues, results, assets, capital spending, and backlog.

title: REPORT OF INDEPENDENT REGISTERED PUBLIC ACCOUNTING FIRM

nodes.title: Boeing Independent Auditor’s Report
nodes.summary: The auditor gives an unqualified opinion that Boeing’s 2021 and 2020 financial position and its results and cash flows for 2019–2021 fairly conform to U.S. GAAP, and reports an unqualified opinion on 2021 internal controls. The report explains management’s and the auditor’s responsibilities, auditor independence, and PCAOB audit procedures designed to provide reasonable assurance against material misstatement. It defines critical audit matters and clarifies they do not change the overall opinion or constitute separate opinions.

nodes.title: Cost Estimates for Fixed-Price Development Contracts – Refer to Notes 1 and 13 to the financial statements
key_items: Critical Audit Matter Description; How the Critical Audit Matter Was Addressed in the Audit
How the Critical Audit Matter Was Addressed in the Audit
nodes.summary: The critical audit matter concerns revenue and margin estimates for fixed-price development contracts, where revenue is recognized over time using costs incurred to measure progress. Estimating costs to completion is uncertain and may lead to lower margins or reach-forward losses, especially for the KC-46A Tanker, Commercial Crew, and VC-25B contracts. Auditing required extensive effort, specialized expertise, and judgment. Procedures assessed management’s methods, assumptions, cost and schedule estimates, project status and challenges, and data accuracy; included site observations and independent outcome expectations; tested related controls; and retrospectively compared actual with estimated performance and financial impacts.

Procedures included assessing management’s delivery and FAA timelines, checking for contradictory information, evaluating delivery-schedule and revenue-estimation methods and assumptions, reviewing customer contracts and expected compensation, and testing related controls and data.

nodes.title: Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Reporting

title: Plan Terms and Eligibility Definitions
summary: Defines the Deferred Compensation Plan (DCP), its pre-2019 deferrals and prior matching contributions, E-Series Payroll (executive levels E-1 to E-5), and positive or negative Earnings Credits. title: 2.31 Eligible Employee
summary: Defines Eligible Employee as a U.S.-payroll Employee who meets applicable requirements for specified deferrals and contribution allocations, is eligible for the Boeing 401(k) but not the Supplemental Savings Plan, and is not employed by an excluded employer listed in Appendix A. Employee means a Controlled Group common-law employee assigned to E-Series Payroll. Extra Deferrals are elected pre-tax base-pay, cash-incentive, or vested-performance-award deferrals. Executive SSP+ Company Contributions are historical amounts credited for periods before January 1, 2022; Incentive Matching Contributions are those allocated under Section 4.3. title: Plan Employee and Contribution Definitions
summary: The page states that Eligible Employees must qualify for the Boeing 401(k), not the Supplemental Savings Plan, and work for an employer not excluded by the Administrator (listed in Appendix A). It defines Employees as Controlled Group common-law employees assigned to E-Series Payroll; Extra Deferrals as specified pre-tax deferrals under Sections 3.1(A) and 3.2(A); Executive SSP+ Company Contributions as historical credits for periods before January 1, 2022; Incentive Matching Contributions as allocations under Section 4.3; and Newly Eligible individuals by recent plan eligibility or distribution history and U.S.-dollar payroll status.

title: Plan Definitions: Participants and Contributions

Restoration Deferrals are elected pre-tax compensation deferrals, Restoration Matching Contributions are amounts credited under Section 4.1, and Restoration SSP+ Company Contributions are historical amounts credited for periods before January 1, 2022.

title: Plan Definitions: Contributions, Service, and Deferrals
summary: Defines Restoration True-Up Contributions and Vested Performance Award Deferrals by reference to plan sections. title: ARTICLE III Participant Deferrals
summary: The article sets eligibility, limits, timing, and administration for annual and mid-year pre-tax Extra and Restoration Deferrals. Extra Deferrals cover Base Pay, cash incentives, and performance awards subject to specified percentage caps; Restoration Deferrals apply after 401(a)(17) or 415(c) limits are reached and mirror Boeing 401(k) contribution percentages. Newly eligible employees may make limited mid-year elections, but not for incentives or awards. Elections may be separate by compensation type, generally carry over unless changed or cancelled, and include distribution choices; legacy elections received specified evergreen treatment. Elections are generally irrevocable after election periods, with limited emergency cancellation, and end for future years when eligibility ceases. Deferrals are credited when compensation would otherwise be paid.

title: ARTICLE IV Company Contributions

nodes.title: Restoration Matching and True-Up Contributions
nodes.summary: Restoration matching contributions are based on the participant’s Boeing 401(k) matching formula and apply only to Base Pay deferred through a timely Restoration Deferral Election, not an Extra Deferral Election; they are credited when the related deferrals are credited. The Company may make discretionary true-up contributions for certain eligible employees to replace matching amounts limited by Code section 415(c). Eligibility does not require a Restoration Deferral Election, but contributions are barred for certain pre-year-end terminations except specified retirement, disability, layoff, or death. True-ups are credited when Boeing 401(k) true-ups are made, or as soon as administratively feasible. Distribution elections are addressed in Article VI.

nodes.title: Incentive Matching and Non-Elective Contributions
key_items: 4.4 Company Non-Elective Contributions (Component of the Executive Benefit)
nodes.summary: Eligible participants who make timely cash incentive deferral elections receive matching contributions based on the Boeing 401(k) matching formula, credited alongside deferrals; none apply to deferrals paid or payable after employment ends. The Company may make non-elective contributions for eligible employees, calculated using the applicable Boeing 401(k) discretionary percentage and eligible compensation. Employees need not defer, but generally must remain employed through the Plan Year’s last business day, except for specified retirement, disability, layoff, or death. Contributions are credited when corresponding Boeing 401(k) contributions are made or as soon as administratively feasible; distribution elections are addressed in Article VI.

nodes.title: 4.5 DC SERP Contributions (Component of the Executive Benefit)
(i) Hired Between January 1, 2009 and December 31, 2019
nodes.summary: DC SERP contributions are available only to eligible employees for a Plan Year, subject to exclusions: none are made for elected officers on or after January 1, 2020, or employees hired or promoted to the E-Series Payroll on or after that date. Employees hired from January 1, 2009, through December 31, 2019, qualify under this subsection if they are currently E-1, E-2, or E-3 and were in E-1 through E-5 on December 31, 2019; are not elected officers; and cannot accrue benefits under a Controlled Group defined benefit plan.

nodes.title: (ii) Hired Before January 1, 2009
nodes.summary: Employees hired before January 1, 2009 qualify under this subsection if they were on the E-series Payroll (E-1 through E-5) on December 31, 2019, and are not elected officers. “Hired” generally means the most recent Company hire or rehire date, subject to exceptions: direct returns from approved leave (including specified ULA/USA transfers) and uninterrupted Controlled Group transfers are not rehires; layoffs followed by rehire within six years generally are not rehires, except when retirement benefits began during that period. Employees becoming group-acquired employees from October 1 through December 31, 2008 are deemed hired on or after January 1, 2009 for later contributions and receive none before that date. Eligible employees participate during periods they meet Section 4.5(A) conditions, and eligible participants may receive contributions as described in the Plan.

nodes.title: (i) Payroll Contributions
nodes.summary: Payroll contributions are credited when Base Pay and Cash Incentive would otherwise be paid, or as soon as administratively feasible. Participants hired from 2009 through 2019 receive a per-pay-period contribution based on eligible pay: 2% at levels E-2 to E-3 or 4% at E-1, using the level held on the period’s last day. Participants hired before 2009 receive 5%, plus a possible age-55 service-based supplement of 0.5% per whole year of Benefit Service, for up to seven aggregate lifetime years under specified start-date rules. For both groups, eligible pay generally requires E-Series Payroll status, with an exception for qualifying post-termination incentive paid by the final regular paycheck.

nodes.title: (ii) One-Time Contribution
nodes.summary: Eligible employees hired from 2009–2019 who are first promoted from E-4/E-5 to E-1–E-3 during a Plan Year receive a one-time contribution equal to 2% of post-promotion base pay plus the cash-incentive target amount, multiplied by whole years of service since their most recent hire date. It is credited at promotion or as soon as administratively feasible; recipients cannot receive another under this provision. Article V outlines vesting and forfeiture rules: Extra Deferral, Restoration, and (subject to stated exceptions) Executive Benefit Accounts are fully vested. The Administrator may forfeit post-2016 legacy Executive SSP+ contributions for qualifying felony misconduct or competition with Controlled Group business during employment or within five years after termination.

The section defines eligibility for DC SERP contributions by hire date, payroll level, officer status, and defined-benefit-plan participation, including rules for rehires, leave, transfers, layoffs, and acquired employees. It explains when eligible periods count and how payroll contributions are credited and calculated for each hire group, including age- and service-based supplements and eligible-pay rules. It also provides a one-time promotion contribution for qualifying 2009–2019 hires and summarizes vesting and potential forfeiture rules for specified accounts and legacy contributions.

nodes.title: Vesting and Forfeiture Rules
nodes.summary: Article V outlines benefit vesting and forfeiture rules, with related provisions on missing participants and improper credits (Section 7.4), anti-assignment (Section 10.2), the Plan’s unfunded status (Section 10.3), and DCP Account forfeitures (Appendix B). Extra Deferral and Restoration Accounts are always 100% vested; Executive Benefit Accounts are also always 100% vested, subject to Sections 5.5 and 5.6.

nodes.title: 5.5 Executive SSP+ Company Contribution Forfeiture Rules
nodes.summary: The Administrator may forfeit some or all legacy Executive SSP+ Company Contributions made on or after January 1, 2017, for misconduct during employment or within five years after termination: conviction for specified felonies or similar harmful unlawful acts; competition with Controlled Group businesses; unauthorized solicitation of workers or contractors; disparaging statements; or misuse/disclosure of confidential information. Protected government communications and sworn testimony are exempt from the latter two rules. The Administrator may recover already-paid amounts through legal or equitable remedies; a court may narrow unenforceable provisions to the broadest enforceable scope. Reimbursement is also required, where appropriate, for contributions tied to incentive awards recovered under a cash-incentive plan clawback.

nodes.title: 5.6 DC SERP Vesting
nodes.summary: DC SERP payments are limited to vested amounts. Participants hired in 2009–2019 generally vest fully after 36 consecutive months in qualifying E-1–E-3 service, employee death, or eligible executive layoff; pre-2009 hires use 36 months on the E-Series Payroll, qualifying death after PVP/BSS vesting, or eligible layoff. For 2009–2019 hires meeting age 55/10 years’ service or 62/1, payroll contributions vest after 36 months and one-time contributions vest 1/36 per qualifying month, subject to death/layoff acceleration. Authorized absences count; other breaks do not aggregate. Certain direct transfers between the Controlled Group and ULA/USA receive comparable executive service credit, subject to conditions. Separation or transfer may forfeit unvested payroll contributions; resumed service affects later one-time accruals, and each account component has separate vesting rules. Forfeitures are not reinstated; related provisions address missing participants, improper credits, anti-assignment, and the plan’s unfunded status.

nodes.title: 5.7 DC SERP Forfeiture Rules
nodes.summary: The Administrator may forfeit some or all of a participant’s DC SERP Account for specified conduct occurring during employment or within five years after termination: qualifying felony misconduct against the Controlled Group; competition or inducing its personnel or contractors to leave or breach contracts without required approval; disparaging statements, except legally protected communications and sworn testimony; or, for contributions made from January 1, 2017, misuse or disclosure of confidential information, subject to the same exceptions. The Administrator may seek legal or equitable recovery of benefits already paid. A court ruling unenforceable provisions narrows them to the broadest enforceable scope. Appropriate forfeiture or reimbursement also applies to account portions tied to incentive awards recovered under a cash-incentive plan’s clawback.

title: ARTICLE VI Distributions

nodes.title: 6.1 Form and Timing of Distribution
nodes.summary: The section sets distribution elections and defaults for Extra Deferral, Restoration, and Executive Benefit Accounts; specifies lump-sum or 2–15-year installment timing, valuation, and earnings rules; and provides a $10,000 installment cash-out. It permits one election change per listed subaccount, subject to advance notice, a 12-month delay, a five-year extension, and age-70½ limits; installment elections cannot change once payments begin. Benefits generally must start by the January following separation and attainment of age 70½. Specified Employees face a six-month payment delay, waived upon death. Unforeseeable-emergency distributions may be made from specified accounts only as needed; DC SERP is excluded.

nodes.title: 6.2 Death Benefits
nodes.summary: If a Participant dies before full distribution of their Account, the remaining balance goes to their Beneficiary according to the Participant’s filed or deemed election, in the same form and at the same time as payments otherwise would have been made (or as soon as practicable after the Company receives notice of death). If the Beneficiary dies before receiving all amounts, unpaid amounts go to their designated beneficiaries under Administrator rules; if none are designated or survive, payment is made to the Beneficiary’s estate in a single lump sum as soon as practicable after death.

nodes.title: 6.3 Rehires and Authorized Periods of Absence/Reduced Level of Services
nodes.summary: Section 6.3 explains benefit payments after rehire or continued employment during an authorized absence or reduced services that constitutes a 409A separation. Forfeited nonvested accounts are not restored on rehire, regardless of later vesting. After benefits begin, Old Account installments continue despite rehire; New Account payments follow the prior election and generally await post-rehire separation. Contributions during qualifying absences are paid the following January if benefits have commenced. Before benefits begin, vested Old Accounts and New Accounts, plus vested contributions during absences, follow prior elections and applicable age/separation timing; resuming service does not change those rules. Election changes remain subject to Section 6.1(F).

summary: The article governs distribution elections and defaults for Extra Deferral, Restoration, and Executive Benefit Accounts, including lump sums or installments, valuation and earnings, small-balance cash-outs, limited election changes, payment timing, age-70½ requirements, six-month delays for Specified Employees, and emergency withdrawals (excluding DC SERP). title: ARTICLE VII Accounts

summary: The Administrator maintains a separate account for each participant and employment period, crediting deferrals, company contributions, and investment earnings and reducing balances for payments. Participants or beneficiaries may elect Interest, Boeing Stock, or designated Other Investment Funds earnings; absent an election, the Interest method applies. The text explains each method’s calculation, stock dividends and adjustments, and possible valuation adjustments. Participants may change future investment directions and transfer funds subject to timing and Boeing Stock Fund restrictions. title: ARTICLE VIII Administration
summary: The Administrator governs the Plan, sets rules and interpretations, makes binding decisions and benefit calculations, may require electronic or telephone elections, and reports periodically to the Compensation Committee. Claims and appeals follow Boeing 401(k) procedures, with the Compensation Committee reviewing elected-officer claims except forfeiture or reimbursement determinations under Sections 5.5 and 5.7; later legal action is subject to Section 10.8. The Board, Compensation Committee, Administrator, and delegates may amend the Plan, including transfers, combinations, or eligibility changes; only the Compensation Committee may change E-Series employee benefit rates or amounts. The Board may terminate the Plan. Benefits upon amendment or termination are protected at the specified baseline, adjusted for Earnings Credits. Distributions generally follow Article VI timing, but Boeing may terminate the entire Plan and pay lump sums as permitted by Code Section 409A and related guidance.

title: ARTICLE X Miscellaneous
key_items: 10.1 No Employment Rights; 10.2 Anti-Assignment; 10.3 Unfunded Status of Plan; 10.4 Delays or Acceleration in Payment; 10.5 Involuntary Inclusion in Income
10.6 Compliance with Code Section 409A; 10.7 Construction; 10.8 Legal Action; 10.9 Tax Withholding
summary: The Plan creates no employment rights and permits termination with or without cause. Benefits cannot be assigned or reached by legal process; attempted transfers may be voided and forfeited, and accounts may cover unreimbursed employer-paid taxes. The Plan is unfunded, though creditor-subject trusts may be established, and participants have only unsecured creditor claims. Payments may be delayed or accelerated under Code section 409A; amounts found currently taxable under that section are immediately distributed, and the Plan is construed to avoid 409A taxation. Federal and Illinois law govern, with invalid provisions severed. Benefit lawsuits must be filed within 180 days after an appeal decision or its deadline; Illinois courts have nonexclusive jurisdiction. Employers may withhold taxes and recover applicable FICA-related amounts, while participants remain responsible for excess tax liabilities. Benefit liability belongs solely to the employing entity unless assumed by another. Overpayments may be offset or otherwise recovered. Notices must be written and hand-delivered or sent by registered or certified mail to specified addresses, and take effect upon delivery or the mailing receipt’s postmark.

summary: The text sets the Plan’s share pool and rules for share sourcing, fractional shares, share recycling, excluded share counts, and alternative compensation awards. It establishes annual limits for participant options/SARs, performance and cash-based awards, nonemployee director awards, awards with limited restrictions, and incentive stock options. It defines eligible employees, directors, and service providers; gives the Committee discretion over award types and documentation; permits compliant payment deferrals and discretionary dividends subject to specified restrictions; and authorizes incentive or nonqualified options, sets a minimum exercise price (except for substitute awards), and prohibits repricing or exchanges without shareholder approval.

title: Eligibility and Award Rules
summary: The Plan caps unrestricted or briefly service-restricted non-option awards at 4 million shares and Incentive Stock Options at 2 million. Eligible persons include selected employees, officers, directors, and natural-person consultants, agents, advisers, or independent contractors providing bona fide services. The Committee chooses award types and may grant them alone or alongside other awards; awards require written documentation. It may permit deferrals under procedures and arrangements compliant with or exempt from Section 409A. It may also credit dividends or equivalents, impose restrictions, and choose payment forms, subject to rules for legacy awards, options and stock appreciation rights, Section 409A, and performance-based vesting and forfeiture.

title: Section 7. Options
summary: The Committee may grant incentive or nonqualified stock options. Exercise prices must generally be at least fair market value on the grant date, with substitute-award exceptions; repricing requires shareholder approval. Options may last up to ten years, with vesting, exercise procedures, whole-share limits, payment methods, and post-termination rights set by the Committee, subject to applicable requirements. Incentive options must comply with Code Section 422, are limited to eligible employees, have an annual $100,000 exercise-value threshold above which options become nonqualified, and may not be granted more than ten years after the Plan’s February 2014 adoption.

title: Section 8. Stock Appreciation Rights
summary: The Committee may grant tandem or freestanding SARs. Tandem grant prices match the related Option; freestanding prices equal grant-date Fair Market Value, except for Substitute Awards. Terms are set by the Committee: freestanding SARs last no more than ten years (or ten years by default), while tandem SARs cannot outlast the Option and are exercisable only for shares then exercisable, upon surrender of equivalent Option rights. Exercise payment equals the excess of exercise-date Fair Market Value over grant price times shares exercised, paid in cash, shares, a combination, or another Committee-approved form. Freestanding SAR instruments specify post-termination exercise terms, subject to possible Committee waiver or modification consistent with Section 409A. Repricing actions require prior shareholder approval.

title: Section 9. Restricted Stock and Stock Units
summary: The Committee may grant Restricted Stock and Stock Units with discretionary terms, conditions, and forfeiture restrictions, including service or performance-based requirements, documented in the award instrument. When restrictions are met or released, Restricted Stock becomes freely transferable, while Stock Units are paid in cash, Common Stock, or both, as determined by the Committee. The Committee may also waive any restrictions or forfeiture periods on terms it considers appropriate.

title: Section 10. Performance Shares, Performance Restricted Stock or Units, and Performance Units
summary: The text authorizes Committee grants of performance share and restricted stock/unit awards payable in stock, with discretionary adjustments or cash substitution, and performance units payable in cash with possible stock substitution. It permits other cash- or stock-based awards, including certain dividends and equivalents. It sets tax and other-obligation withholding methods and bars assignment of awards except inheritance or permitted beneficiary designation. It preserves corporate-action authority and liability protections, and requires equitable adjustments for specified transactions affecting shares or award value.

title: Awards, Withholding, and Transfer Restrictions
key_items: Section 11. Other Stock or Cash-Based Awards
summary: The Committee may adjust Performance Unit consideration or substitute stock for cash, and grant other cash- or stock-based incentives, including certain legacy dividends and equivalents. The Company may require payment of taxes and other debts before issuing shares; the Committee may allow or require payment in cash, cash withholding, share withholding, or surrender of owned shares. Awards generally cannot be transferred or pledged, except by inheritance or permitted beneficiary designation; they are exercisable during the participant’s life only by the participant or, if legally incapacitated, a legal representative, and are protected from creditor process.

title: Section 14. Adjustments
summary: Section 14 preserves the Company’s and shareholders’ authority to undertake corporate actions without claims by participants or others. It requires equitable Award adjustments for specified distributions, capital changes, transactions, or events to prevent dilution or enlargement of benefits. For defined Corporate Transactions—including a 50% voting-power acquisition, substantially-all-assets sale, qualifying merger, or Incumbent Board majority loss—the Board may provide value-preserving substitute awards, cancel options or stock appreciation rights for any positive transaction-price excess over exercise costs, and fairly adjust or settle other Awards; replacement awards or payments cancel affected Awards without consent. Unvested Awards do not automatically vest. The section also defines transaction price, including Board good-faith valuation of noncash consideration consistent with applicable law.

title: Section 15. Amendment and Termination
summary: The Board or Committee may amend, suspend, or terminate the Plan, subject to shareholder approval when required by law, NYSE rules, or for material revisions—including changes weakening anti-repricing protections or increasing shares available. The Plan ends ten years after shareholder approval unless ended sooner; no new Awards may then be granted, though existing Awards continue under their terms. Incentive Stock Options cannot be granted more than ten years after the Board’s February 2014 adoption. Changes generally may not materially harm participants’ existing Award rights or jeopardize ISO qualification without consent, except adjustments under Section 14.

title: Section 16. General
summary: Section 16 sets general Plan terms: Awards are subject to Board clawback policy and may be forfeited or recovered for specified misconduct within two years of later vesting or payment, subject to law and exceptions, including deductions from future compensation; protected government communications and sworn testimony are excluded. Participants have no right to Awards or continued employment, and Awards do not create employment contracts. Share issuance is conditional on legal and exchange compliance; the Company need not register securities and may impose transfer restrictions or issue shares electronically. Covered Board members, committee members, and authorized officers receive conditional indemnification. Award holders generally have no shareholder rights before share issuance. The Committee may tailor rules for Section 16 compliance, ISO and Section 409A treatment, including amendments and payment delays. It may adopt foreign-country modifications and qualifying price-averaging methods. The Plan is unfunded, participants are unsecured creditors, successor companies inherit obligations, invalid provisions may be modified or severed, and Delaware law governs unless otherwise specified.

title: Section 17. Restatement Effective Date
summary:

This amendment and restatement of the Plan shall be effective December 9, 2021.
